content_html:
Before your next virtual event or job interview, a quick online webcam test shows you exactly what everyone else is about to see. It runs free in your browser with no sign-up, then reports your supported resolutions, real FPS, sharpness, noise and lighting, so you can fix a dark or choppy video before anyone joins.

How the Webcam Test Tool Measures Webcam Resolution and Frame Rate

When you press start, the webcam test tool first checks that your browser can reach your media devices. Once you allow access, it opens a live video stream in the webcam viewer and reads its abilities through the MediaStreamTrack getCapabilities() method. It then reports the model name, any built-in microphone, the video standard, an estimated bitrate, the bandwidth a call will need and the number of colors in a captured frame.

The megapixel figure comes straight from the reported resolution:

$$\text{Megapixels} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height}}{1{,}000{,}000}$$

Say the readout shows 2560 × 1440 at 24 frames per second. That works out to \( \frac{2560 \times 1440}{1{,}000{,}000} = 3.69 \) megapixels. At 24 fps each frame lasts \( 1000 \div 24 = 41.7 \) ms, and the sensor pushes about 88.5 million pixels every second, which is why call apps compress the picture heavily before sending it.

Max Resolution, Supported Resolutions and Aspect Ratio

The tool steps through common sizes and keeps the largest one that actually works: its max resolution. Most webcams can't do 4K, and a refused size is marked unsupported rather than faked. A dedicated webcam resolution tester goes further and logs each size with its top speed. The aspect ratio is width over height in lowest terms, so 2560 × 1440 reduces to 16:9, the shape call apps expect.

NameWidth × heightShapeMP
VGA640 × 4804:30.31
HD1280 × 72016:90.92
Full HD1920 × 108016:92.07
QHD (worked example)2560 × 144016:93.69
4K UHD3840 × 216016:98.29

Why FPS Matters on Video Calls

Frame speed decides how smooth you look. A healthy webcam holds 24 to 30 frames each second; below about 15, motion stutters and you get video lags. A low frame rate is usually a symptom, not a fault: in a dim room the sensor holds each exposure longer, so 24 in daylight can fall to 15 at night, stretching each frame from 41.7 ms to 66.7 ms. Test your webcam in the room and light you'll actually call from, especially before streaming to an audience.

Picture Quality and Image Quality Readings

Beyond size and speed, the test samples a frame for brightness, saturation and overall color balance. Very few colors usually points to poor light or a cheap sensor, while a grayscale feed can mean a power-saving mode or another app muting the image.

How to Test Your Webcam Online in a Few Clicks

You don't need to install any software. The whole check runs in a browser tab:

  1. Press the Test my cam button at the top of the page.
  2. When the browser pop-up asks for permission, click Allow so the page can start the stream.
  3. Watch the live camera feed. If you see yourself, it works; if the window stays black, see the troubleshooting section below.
  4. Read the results table for size, speed and color, then judge the image quality yourself: sharp edges, natural skin tones and no smearing when you move.
  5. Switch cameras from the menu if you have more than one, and test each.
  6. Grab a few snapshots or open fullscreen to inspect fine detail, then record video for a few seconds to check sound and motion together.

With nothing installed, it's the quickest way to check camera online on a shared computer, and to test webcam output again after a driver update.

A Tutor Uses the Webcam Viewer to Pick Between Two Cameras

It's 6:40 pm, twenty minutes before a 90-minute online chemistry lesson, and I need to decide one thing: use the laptop's built-in camera, or the 1080p plug-in camera I bought last week so students can read my whiteboard? The answer turned out to be the new camera, but only after adding a lamp.

I open the test, select the built-in camera first and allow access. The readout shows 1280 × 720 at 30 frames each second: 0.92 MP, 33.3 ms per frame. Then I switch to the plug-in camera. It reports 1920 × 1080, 2.07 MP, but only 13 frames each second under the overhead light, so each frame hangs for 76.9 ms. In the preview my hand smears every time I write.

What stands out comes from reading the two test results together: size times speed gives 27.6 million pixels a second for the built-in camera and only 27.0 million for the "better" one. Below about 14 frames each second (27.648 ÷ 2.0736 = 13.3), the sharper camera delivers less picture, not more.

SetupSizeSpeedms per frameM pixels/s
Built-in, ceiling light1280 × 7203033.327.6
Plug-in, ceiling light1920 × 10801376.927.0
Plug-in, desk lamp added1920 × 10802737.056.0

So I change one input: a desk lamp aimed at the whiteboard, nothing else. The rerun shows 27 frames each second, 37.0 ms per frame and 56.0 million pixels a second, comfortably above the 24 frames-per-second film standard. Writing stays crisp in the preview, and that decides it.

One caveat I'd flag for anyone doing the same check: many plug-in cameras have a low-light compensation setting that deliberately lowers the frame speed to brighten the picture. Switching it off in the maker's app brings the speed back without a lamp, but adds visible grain, so light is the better fix. Also, the readout shows what the camera delivers to the browser; most call apps then downscale, so the 1080p advantage on the call is smaller than the test suggests. The input I'd watch first is light, because it moved the result more than the camera upgrade did.

Webcam Not Working? Web Camera Troubleshooting

A web camera that shows a black screen or an error usually fails in one of three places: blocked access, a busy device or a connection fault. Corporate firewalls can also block inputs inside a browser, so try a home network too.

Camera Permission and Camera Access in Chrome and Safari

Clicked Block by mistake? The browser remembers it:

  • Chrome: click the icon left of the address bar, open site settings, set Camera to Allow and reload.
  • Safari: open the Websites pane, choose Camera and pick Allow next to this site.
  • Firefox and Edge: click the camera icon in the address bar and remove the block.

Camera permission can also be blocked one level up. Windows privacy settings and macOS System Settings both have a per-app switch; if your browser isn't ticked there, no website can get camera access.

Another App or Multiple Cameras

Usually only one program can hold a webcam at a time. If Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Skype or OBS is open, quit it fully and rerun. With multiple cameras (a built-in one, a plug-in model, a virtual camera from streaming software or an iPhone through Continuity Camera) the browser may pick the wrong one, so choose from the list, the same way you pick front/back cameras on a phone.

External Webcam Drivers, USB and Hardware Failure

For an external webcam, check that the plug is fully seated, try a different USB port and look for damage along the connection cable. On Windows, open Device Manager or the Control Panel devices view to confirm it's listed, and update its drivers there or from the maker's site. If it still fails on another computer, it's a hardware failure and no setting will fix it.

Webcam Tester Fixes for Grainy or Blurry Video Quality

A working webcam can still look bad. Most video quality problems trace back to light, a smudged cover glass or another app forcing a lower mode. Raising contrast in a filter panel only helps once the light is right.

Grainy Video and Lighting Conditions

Poor lighting conditions force the sensor to amplify a weak signal, which shows up as speckled noise and muddy color. Face the light source rather than sitting with it behind you; even a small desk lamp can lift a feed back to full speed. Then rerun the test: the speed reading should climb back and the speckle fade. If it doesn't, another app may be forcing a smaller size.

Blurry Picture: Clean the Lens

Fingerprints and dust stop autofocus from locking on. Wipe the glass with a microfiber cloth, and sit at least 50 cm back so autofocus can focus properly.

Test Your Camera on Windows 10, macOS and Linux

The browser check works on every major operating system, including Linux and Android, on any smartphone or tablet, in a current Chrome, Firefox or Edge. Test your camera online first, then fall back to the built-in apps below.

Laptop Webcam and the Windows 10 Camera App

A laptop webcam needs no install. Open the Camera app from the Start menu then take photos or record video and compare the image with the browser's. If the app works but the browser doesn't, the issue is access, not the webcam itself.

Photo Booth on Mac and Logitech Webcams

On a Mac, open Photo Booth from Applications; if your picture appears there, the webcam is fine. For a Logitech model, adjust exposure or white balance in the maker's free companion app, then rerun the browser test to compare readings.

Webcam Testing for Video Conferencing: Framing and Privacy

Before a webinar, a Google Meet client call or a family video call, a webcam testing tool run five minutes ahead removes the guesswork.

Mirror View, Natural View and Eye Level

Most tools show mirror view by default, like a selfie. Switch to natural view to see the unflipped picture others get, which matters if you hold up text. Set the lens at or just above eye level, tilted slightly down, and use a rule-of-thirds grid to put your eyes on the upper line with a little space above your head.

Private, Secure and Free With No Sign-Up

A good browser test processes everything locally: no video, picture or metadata leaves your device, and nothing is stored once you close the stream. No account or card is needed.

faq.question: Why should I test my webcam before a video call?
faq.answer: Testing your webcam beforehand ensures there are no technical issues — like a frozen feed, poor lighting, or low frame rate — that could disrupt a meeting or interview. A quick check gives you confidence that you'll appear clearly and professionally on the other end.

faq.question: How does the online webcam test work?
faq.answer: The tool uses your browser's built-in media APIs to request access to your camera. Once you grant permission, it reads properties like resolution, frame rate, and device info directly from the video stream. No footage is recorded or uploaded — everything stays on your device.

faq.question: Why does my webcam test appear to fail or show no image?
faq.answer: Common causes include: the camera not being plugged in securely, browser permissions being blocked, or outdated drivers. Try refreshing the page, clicking 'Allow' when the browser prompts for camera access, or testing in a different browser. If you're using an external USB webcam, try a different USB port.

faq.question: Which devices and browsers are compatible with this webcam test?
faq.answer: The tool works on any modern browser — Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari — across laptops, desktops, smartphones, and tablets. Make sure your browser is up to date to ensure full support for camera APIs.

faq.question: What do frame rate (FPS) and bitrate mean for webcam quality?
faq.answer: Frame rate (FPS) measures how many image frames your webcam captures per second — higher FPS means smoother video. Bitrate refers to the amount of data processed per second; a higher bitrate generally means sharper, more detailed video but requires more bandwidth.

faq.question: How can I fix poor webcam image quality like low saturation or bad lighting?
faq.answer: Start by improving your room lighting — natural light from in front of you works best. In your webcam's settings (accessible via the camera app or video software), you can often adjust brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue. Some webcams also have companion desktop software with fine-grained controls.

faq.question: Does this tool record or store my webcam footage?
faq.answer: No. This tool does not record, transmit, or store any video from your webcam. The camera stream is processed entirely within your browser for testing purposes only. Your privacy is fully protected.

faq.question: What's the difference between integrated, USB, and wireless webcams?
faq.answer: Integrated webcams are built directly into laptops and tablets — convenient but typically lower quality. USB webcams plug into a port and generally offer better resolution and frame rates. Wireless webcams connect via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, offering cable-free flexibility but requiring a stable wireless connection.

content_html:
Asking what camera do I have, and what your web camera can actually do? Run the Camera Information Report and your browser will test your camera in seconds, then list its device name, real resolution, FPS and aspect ratio, plus the light and colour readings that decide how you look on video calls or when streaming. Nothing to install: the report reads the webcam and its microphone straight through the browser.

What the Camera Information Report Shows

The report turns what your camera tells the browser into one table of specifications. Every row below is measured from the live stream, not copied from the box, which is why the webcam information here can differ from the seller's listing.

Report fieldWhat it tells you
Webcam NameThe label your operating system gives the webcam
Quality RatingA summary score built from resolution, colours and smoothness
Built-in Microphone / Built-in SpeakerWhether the camera also exposes audio devices
Frame RateHow many frames per second the stream delivers
Stream Type / Image ModeLive video or a still source; colour or black and white
Webcam MegaPixels / Webcam ResolutionPixel size of each frame
Video Standard / Aspect RatioThe named format (VGA, Full HD, 4K) and the frame shape
PNG File Size / JPEG File SizeHow large one captured snapshot is in each format
BitrateApproximate bandwidth the stream needs
Number of Colors / Average RGB ColorColour richness and the overall tint of the frame
Lightness, Luminosity, Brightness, Hue, SaturationHow exposed and how vivid the image is

Webcam Name and Built-in Microphone Detection

The webcam name is the device name the system registers, so it is the quickest way to confirm which camera the browser picked when an external webcam and a built-in one are both connected. The report also flags a built-in microphone or built-in speaker on the same webcam camera; treat that row as a hint, because some drivers report audio devices loosely.

Webcam Resolution, Megapixels and Aspect Ratio

The webcam resolution is the largest frame size the camera streams, and two other rows are derived from it:

$$\text{Megapixels} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height}}{1{,}000{,}000}$$

Take a 2K webcam reporting 2560 × 1440. That is 3,686,400 pixels, or 3.69 megapixels. Dividing both sides by their greatest common divisor (160) gives 16 × 9, so the aspect ratio is 16:9 and the video standard is QHD (1440p). Each frame carries four times the pixels of a 1280 × 720 HD camera, and a single megapixel more or less is easy to see in the comparison below.

  • VGA, 640 × 480: 0.31 MP, 4:3
  • 1080p, 1920 × 1080: 2.07 MP, 16:9
  • QHD, 2560 × 1440: 3.69 MP, 16:9
  • 4K UHD, 3840 × 2160: 8.29 MP, 16:9

Frame Rate and Video Standard

The same 2K webcam delivering 24 frames per second paints a new frame every 41.7 ms. Uncompressed, 3,686,400 pixels × 24 bits × 24 frames is about 2.12 Gbit/s, which is why every video conferencing app compresses the stream; the report's bitrate row estimates the bandwidth that compressed stream will use. The video standard row simply names the format the resolution matches.

Image Quality and Number of Colors

For image quality, the report samples a frame and counts the number of colors in it: more colours usually mean better optics and better light. Brightness, lightness and luminosity show exposure, while hue and saturation show tint and vividness. A frame with very few colours, or one stuck in black and white, points to poor light or a muted stream.

How to Test Your Webcam and Read the Results

To test your webcam, this free webcam test runs in four steps, and you can repeat it for each camera you own:

  1. Pick the camera from the device list if you have more than one, then click "Test my webcam".
  2. Click Allow when Chrome, Safari or Firefox asks to use the camera.
  3. Watch the webcam viewer: if you can see yourself, the video track is live.
  4. Wait for the table to fill, then take snapshots or switch to fullscreen to check the picture.

Run it again whenever you plug in a new camera; the webcam testing tool resets for each device you check your webcam with.

Camera Access and Browser Permissions

No report appears until the browser has camera access. If you clicked Block by mistake, reset the browser permissions:

  • Chrome and Edge: click the icon left of the address bar, set Camera to Allow, then reload.
  • Firefox: click the camera icon in the address bar and remove the blocked permission.
  • Safari: open Settings, choose Websites, then Camera, and set this site to Allow.

Chrome, Firefox and Safari only ask once per site: allow the camera here and you can revoke it later from the same settings.

How the Maximum Resolution Is Detected

Browsers don't announce a camera's limits directly. The tool lists your media devices, then requests progressively larger frame sizes and keeps the largest supported resolution the camera accepts. That size is the maximum resolution, which can sit below the box figure if the USB connection or the driver caps it.

Checking a Web Camera's Frame Rate Before an Evening Lesson

I teach maths online at 7:30 pm, and students keep telling me my whiteboard writing looks smeared. Before buying a new camera, I want to know whether the laptop's built-in 1080p camera is the problem. After three runs of the report, the answer is clear: the camera is fine, the room is too dark, and the darkness is halving the frame rate.

At 7:15 pm, with only the ceiling light on, I start the test and let the table fill. The webcam information shows 1920 × 1080, 2.07 MP and 16:9, so resolution isn't what's smearing the board. The Frame Rate row reads 14.9 fps: one new frame every 67.1 ms, roughly twice the 33.4 ms interval of the 29.97 fps NTSC rate most webcams are built around. A marker stroke drawn mid-frame simply blurs.

The cause is auto-exposure. A sensor can't deliver frames faster than it collects light, so the ceiling is:

$$\text{max frame rate} = \frac{1}{\text{exposure time}}$$

If the camera needs 1/15 s (66.7 ms) per frame in that light, 15 is its limit, which matches the 14.9 reading almost exactly. To rule out a busy computer, I close every other app and rerun, then switch on a desk lamp and rerun once more:

SetupFrame rateTime per frame
Ceiling light only14.9 fps67.1 ms
Ceiling light, other apps closed14.8 fps67.6 ms
Desk lamp facing me29.8 fps33.6 ms

Closing apps changes nothing; the lamp doubles the frame rate. So I keep the laptop camera and move the lamp to my desk permanently, which costs nothing.

The number to watch here is the frame rate, not the megapixels. A slow reading looks exactly like a weak computer, and plenty of people upgrade a webcam that was only starved of light. Two caveats: run the report in the light you will actually teach in, because a noon test would have shown 30 fps and hidden the problem; and if the rate stays near 15 even under bright light, check the camera's driver software for a low-light mode, which deliberately trades frame rate for brightness, before you blame the hardware.

Why a Webcam Test Fails

When the viewer stays black, the cause is nearly always one of these, so work through them in order:

  • Camera blocked: you clicked Block instead of Allow; reset it as shown above.
  • Camera busy: Zoom, Teams or Google Meet is holding the camera, so close them and reload.
  • Disabled in system settings: check the camera switch in Windows or macOS privacy settings.
  • Drivers: on Windows, update them in Device Manager, or get them from the maker's site.
  • Connection: reseat the cable or try another USB port.
  • Hardware: if it fails on a second computer too, the camera is faulty.

Troubleshooting order matters: permission first, software next, hardware last, because each step rules out the cheapest fix before an expensive one.

Grayscale and Low Resolution Warnings

Even a working camera can trigger a warning. A low frame rate usually means an overloaded system or poor light, since many webcams slow the shutter in the dark. A low resolution warning means the camera, or a setting in the operating system, is capping the frame size. Grayscale output, a single-colour frame or a frozen image suggests a power-saving mode or another app muting the stream, while heavy noise levels point back to lighting.

Checking a Laptop Webcam on Windows and macOS

The report works on any laptop, desktop or smartphone with a modern browser, whether it runs Windows, ChromeOS or Linux. To cross-check a laptop webcam outside the browser:

  • On Windows, open the Camera app from the Start menu and take a test photo.
  • On macOS, open Photo Booth and record a short clip.
  • For a branded camera, use the maker's own settings app to adjust focus and exposure.

If the camera app works but the browser doesn't, the problem is browser permission, not the webcam.

Video Quality Before Video Calls

Run the report about ten minutes before a webinar or other virtual events, in the room you'll actually use. Check video quality under your real lighting conditions: image sharpness, color balance and a smooth picture matter more on screen than an extra megapixel. A quick video recording played back afterwards shows you what other people will see.

Privacy When You Check Your Webcam Online

An online webcam test should never need to upload your face. Here, every camera and microphone measurement runs locally in the browser and the stream stays in your device's memory; nothing is recorded or stored, and closing the tab discards it. Results are estimates that depend on the browser and driver, so if a number looks wrong, rerun the webcam test online in a second browser before trusting it. That also makes the cam test a fair way to compare two cameras side by side.

faq.question: What does the camera information report show?
faq.answer: It lists your webcam's device name, maximum resolution, megapixels, aspect ratio, video standard, frame rate, image mode, built-in microphone and colour and brightness readings, all measured from the live stream rather than taken from the box.

faq.question: Why is my webcam's resolution lower than advertised?
faq.answer: The report shows the largest frame size the camera actually accepts through your browser. A USB port, hub, driver or system setting can cap it below the figure on the box.

faq.question: Why is my frame rate low?
faq.answer: Most often the room is too dark: auto-exposure lengthens each frame, and frame rate can't exceed one divided by the exposure time. A busy computer is the other cause, so close other apps and retest.

faq.question: Why can't the test find my camera?
faq.answer: Check that the browser has permission to use the camera, that no app such as Zoom or Teams is holding it, that it isn't disabled in Windows or macOS privacy settings, and that its cable and drivers are fine.

faq.question: How do I allow camera access in my browser?
faq.answer: Click Allow when the browser asks. If you blocked it, use the icon beside the address bar in Chrome, Edge or Firefox, or Safari's Websites settings, to set Camera to Allow, then reload.

faq.question: Is my video uploaded during the test?
faq.answer: No. The measurements run locally in your browser and the stream stays in your device's memory; closing the page discards it.

content_html:
The box your webcam came in might promise a sharp picture, but the number that matters is the one it actually delivers to your browser. This maximum resolution detector runs a webcam resolution test on your laptop or computer and lists every one of your supported resolutions, so you see your true webcam max resolution, the real ceiling on image quality, whether you use a built-in webcam or a plug-in one.

How the Maximum Resolution Detector Finds Your Webcam's Limits

When you press start, the tool asks your webcam for one size after another and reads back what the video track really sends. Results fill in in real time, and you can scan resolutions again after changing cameras or browsers.

Resolution Standards vs the Brute-Force Method

By default the scan checks common resolution standards such as VGA, HD and FHD. That's quick, but a camera can also support non-standard resolutions that aren't on the list. Turn on the brute-force method to step through sizes one at a time. It takes longer, but it catches odd sizes. If your browser applies downscaling, it shrinks the output, and the list can come back shorter than what the camera really supports.

Default Resolution vs Maximum Supported Resolution

The tool reports three numbers. The default resolution is what your browser picks when a site opens the camera without asking for a size. The maximum supported resolution is the largest size the sensor will deliver. The minimum resolution is the smallest. Apps often start at the default, so a 5 MP camera can still appear on a call at 0.31 MP.

Webcam Resolution in Pixels and Megapixels

A resolution is two numbers: the width and the height in pixels. Multiply them to get the total pixel count, then divide by one million for the megapixel figure that manufacturers put on the box. Here's how the common sizes compare:

StandardDimensionsTotal countMegapixels
VGA640 × 480307,2000.31
HD (720p)1280 × 720921,6000.92
FHD (1080p)1920 × 10802,073,6002.07
QHD2560 × 14403,686,4003.69
4K Ultra HD3840 × 21608,294,4008.29

Camera Resolution Formula With a Worked Example

The figure on the box always comes from the same formula:

$$\text{MP} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height}}{1{,}000{,}000}$$

Say the scan reports a top size of 2592 × 1944. That's \(2592 \times 1944 = 5{,}038{,}848\) pixels, or 5.04 MP, so the sensor really is a 5 MP part. The same scan shows a default of 640 × 480 (0.31 MP) and a minimum of 160 × 120 (0.02 MP), which means apps that keep the default use about 1/16 of what this camera can capture.

Frame Rate and Max FPS From 720p to 4K

Resolution tells you how sharp each frame is. Frame rate, measured in frames per second, tells you how smooth the motion looks. Most USB links have a bandwidth ceiling, so the camera trades one for the other, and the fps checker records the top rate for every size. Here's the same 5 MP camera from the example above:

ResolutionMP per frameHighest fps
640 × 4800.3160
1280 × 7200.9260
1920 × 10802.0730
2304 × 12962.9920
2592 × 19445.0415

At 15 fps the top size is fine for still shots, but 1080p at 30 fps is the smoother choice for live video.

Why Lighting Lowers Your Frame Rate

In a dim room the camera keeps each frame exposed for longer, so the top fps the scan records will read low, even at sizes the camera supports. Run the test in good lighting to see the real figures. Better light also cuts noise, which lowers the file size of a recording and improves video quality.

Using the Webcam Test to Set Up a Handwriting Camera

A maths tutor wants to point an external webcam straight down at the desk so students can read worked solutions in real time. The question is simple: will a 4 mm handwritten digit stay legible? The short answer turns out to be yes, but only at the camera's top size and only if the call app doesn't shrink it.

The box says "2K". The detector's first scan reports a default of 640 × 480, and the brute-force pass then finds a maximum resolution of 2688 × 1512 at 15 fps. That's \(2688 \times 1512 = 4{,}064{,}256\), or 4.06 MP. On the arm the tutor has, the frame covers 236 mm of the page vertically, so the vertical detail is 1512 ÷ 236 = 6.41 pixels per mm. A 4 mm digit is about 25.6 pixels tall. To cross-check, the tutor takes a still photo at that size and counts the rows across one digit, and the number matches.

Rows usedPixels per mmEquivalent dpi4 mm digit height
7203.0577.512.2 px
10804.58116.218.3 px
15126.41162.725.6 px

The 1512 rows the detector reported are the hard ceiling here. For context, 300 dpi, the usual standard for document scans, works out to 11.81 pixels per mm. To reach it with 1512 rows, the frame could be no taller than 128 mm, which would cut off half the worksheet. The tutor settles on a 165 mm frame instead (9.16 px/mm, about 233 dpi), which still covers the full 210 mm page width in a 16:9 shot.

The catch most people miss is that the detector measures what the camera hands the browser, not what the call sends. Many meeting apps send 720p by default, which drops the same digit to about 12 pixels on the student's screen. My judgement here is that the number to watch is the call app's outgoing setting, not the sensor. The tutor's next step is to turn on the app's HD video option and test again with a student before the first lesson. As a fallback, the tutor can send a full-size photo of the finished page.

Picture Quality Beyond Camera Resolution

A higher number doesn't guarantee better picture quality. The optics and the sensor decide how much of that resolution holds real detail in your video.

Why the Highest Resolution Isn't Always the Sharpest

A cheap sensor pushed to its top size often adds noise and compression blocks, so its sharpness can fall behind a good Full HD camera. For everyday video calls, clean 1080p usually gives better clarity than a noisy higher setting. A 4K webcam only looks better when the optics in front of the sensor can resolve that much detail.

Glass Lens and Field of View

The lens limits detail before resolution does. A glass lens renders crisper edges than a plastic one, which is why most cameras rated at Full HD and above use glass, and why it gives crisper video. The field of view matters too: a wide angle spreads the same detail across a bigger scene, so your face takes up less of the frame. The detector reports which sizes the sensor supports, not how good the optics are, so two models with the same top size can still show very different detail.

How to Use the Resolution Tester

You can check webcam resolution in a minute. Nothing leaves your machine:

  1. Open this webcam test and click Allow when your browser asks for camera permissions.
  2. If you have more than one camera, choose the right one from the drop-down list.
  3. Start the scan and watch each size get marked supported or unsupported.
  4. Optionally take photos at each size to compare detail side by side.
  5. Close the webcam stream when you're done.

For privacy, the whole test runs locally, and no frame or metadata is uploaded.

Test Multiple Webcams and Export Results

Repeat the scan for a built-in webcam, an external webcam or a usb webcam to compare them. You can export each run as CSV or JSON to keep a record or send it to IT support.

When the Webcam Tester Reports the Wrong Max Resolution

If the webcam tester shows a lower max resolution than the spec sheet promises, it's usually a setup problem, not the sensor.

Camera Permission Denied or Camera in Use

If permission was blocked at the browser or operating system level, the webcam resolution tester gets no stream at all, so reset site permissions and check your system privacy settings. On Windows, Zoom, Teams or OBS can hold the camera exclusively, so close them first.

Wrong Camera or Virtual Camera Selected

Software like OBS adds a virtual camera that reports its own sizes, not your hardware's. A phone linked as a webcam can do the same. Pick the physical webcam by name before you run the scan.

Grainy or Blurry Image After a Resolution Test

A grainy picture at a supported size usually means another video app forced a lower setting, or there isn't enough light. A blurry picture points to a smudged lens, so wipe it before you test again.

faq.question: How does a maximum resolution detector find my webcam's top size?
faq.answer: It asks the camera for one resolution after another and reads back the size the video track actually delivers, then marks each one supported or not. The largest supported size is your maximum resolution.

faq.question: Why is my default resolution lower than the maximum?
faq.answer: Browsers and many apps open the camera at a small default, often 640 × 480, unless a site asks for more. The camera can still deliver its maximum once a larger size is requested.

faq.question: What does the brute-force method do?
faq.answer: The quick scan only checks popular resolution standards. Brute-force steps through widths and heights up to a limit (2048 pixels by default) so non-standard resolutions your camera supports aren't missed. It is slower but more complete.

faq.question: How are megapixels calculated from a resolution?
faq.answer: Multiply width by height and divide by one million. A 1920 × 1080 Full HD webcam captures 2,073,600 pixels, which is about 2 MP.

faq.question: Does a higher resolution always mean better picture quality?
faq.answer: No. Resolution sets how many pixels each frame has, but the lens, sensor and lighting decide how much real detail you get. A clean Full HD image often looks better than a noisy higher setting.

faq.question: Why does my webcam show fewer resolutions than its spec sheet?
faq.answer: Another app may be holding the camera, the wrong camera or a virtual camera may be selected, or the browser may be downscaling the output. Close other video apps, pick the physical camera and scan again.

faq.question: Is the webcam resolution test private?
faq.answer: Yes. The scan runs locally in your browser after you grant camera permission, and no video, picture or metadata is uploaded.

h1: Mobile Camera Test: Free Phone Camera & Webcam Test Online
subtitle: Tap Front Camera or Rear Camera on this mobile camera test to see each lens's real Resolution.

card.fields_html:
Camera Preview

Switch between your front and rear cameras

Your camera feed will appear here
—Active Facing
—Resolution
—Frame Rate
—Screen Orientation
Tap Front Camera or Rear Camera to begin.

Lenses Tested This Session

Every distinct camera your browser has reported so far

No lens tested yet — switch cameras above to populate this table.

iPhones running Safari report exactly one front and one rear entry, no matter how many physical lenses the phone has — this is a browser limitation, not a bug. Android/Chromium phones usually report more, though some manufacturers group several lenses into one entry.

content_html:
Before you trust a phone with an interview or a second-hand purchase, run this mobile camera test. It opens a live preview of your phone camera right in the browser, a free camera test with no download, and checks the front and rear lenses for blur, grain and poor lighting. You get the real resolution and frames per second each camera streams before your next video calls.

How the Mobile Camera Test Works in Your Browser

The test asks the browser for a video stream, shows it in real time, and reads the stream's settings back from the device. With no software to install, camera testing this way takes seconds, and the same page works as a webcam tester on a computer.

Allow Camera Access When Prompted

Tap Start and your phone shows a camera permission prompt. Choose Allow. Tap Block and you must reset it in the site settings. Browsers only hand the camera to a secure HTTPS page, so a plain http:// copy of any camera tool never gets a picture.

Switch Between the Front Camera and Rear Camera

Use the switch control to move between the selfie lens and the main camera on the back. The page requests each one by its facing mode, user for the front and environment for the back, so a camera that never appears usually means the phone is not exposing it to web pages, not that it is broken.

Capture a Test Photo or Short Clip

A still frame tells you more than the preview. Capture one, open it in fullscreen and zoom into the corners, where smudges and soft edges show up first. Most tools save the frame as a JPEG or PNG, and a short recording shows whether the picture stutters when you pan.

Privacy: Nothing Leaves Your Phone

The video is processed on your device and never uploaded. Close the tab and the stream stops. That is the whole security model: no account and no server copy.

Reading Your Phone Camera Results

The readout describes the stream the browser negotiated, not the sensor on the spec sheet. Take a phone sold as 50 MP on the back and 12 MP on the front. A sample run gives these numbers:

ReadoutRear cameraFront camera
Stream resolution1920 × 1440960 × 720
Stream size2.76 MP0.69 MP
Share of sensor rating5.5% of 50 MP5.8% of 12 MP
Aspect ratio4:34:3
Frame rate (8-second sample)29.8 (238 frames)18.4 in a dim room, 29.5 under a lamp

Camera Resolution and Megapixels

Megapixels in the readout come straight from the stream size:

$$\text{MP} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height}}{1{,}000{,}000}$$

For the back camera that is 1920 × 1440 ÷ 1,000,000 = 2.76 MP, about 5.5% of the number on the box. That is normal: phones combine sensor pixels and the browser asks for a video mode, so judge the result against video tiers instead: 720p HD, 1080p and 4K. A short side under 720 pixels is a real warning sign. The 960 × 720 front stream just clears it.

Frame Rate and FPS Stability

The test counts frames over a few seconds and divides by the time:

$$\text{frames per second} = \frac{\text{frames counted}}{\text{seconds}}$$

238 frames in 8 seconds gives 29.8, effectively the 30 frames per second phones aim for. The front one managing only 18.4 in a dim room is not faulty. Each frame needs a longer exposure (54 ms instead of 34 ms), so fewer of them fit into a second. A rate that stays low in good conditions hurts video quality and streaming far more than a lower resolution does.

Aspect Ratio and Orientation

Most phone sensors are 4:3, so a 4:3 stream is expected. A 16:9 result means the phone is cropping for video. Turn the phone and the numbers swap (1440 × 1920 in portrait). The picture is scaled to fit your display, so read the numbers, not the size of the image on screen.

Check Camera Quality: Sharpness, Exposure and Noise

The numbers confirm the camera works. Your eyes confirm the image quality. Point the phone at fine print and a plain wall.

Blurry Preview or Soft Focus

A blurry picture is usually a smudged lens. Wipe it with a dry cloth and test again. If text still will not sharpen at arm's length, tap to focus, and if autofocus keeps hunting, the module may be damaged. Wide-aperture phone cameras have a shallow depth of field up close, and optical stabilization can make the preview wobble briefly. Both are normal.

Low Light, Brightness and Exposure

Test once in a normal room and once with the lamp off. In low light the phone lengthens exposure and raises gain, so frames per second drop and grain appears. A picture that stays dark or washed out in a well-lit room points to an exposure fault instead. The flash cannot be checked on every phone: iOS does not let web pages switch the torch on.

Mirror View vs the Saved Image

The front preview is usually shown as a mirror image, the way a selfie looks to you. People on a video call see the unflipped picture, and most saved frames are unflipped too, so text on your shirt reading backwards in the preview is not a fault. Use the flip toggle to see what others see. Webcam previews behave the same way.

Vetting a $185 Used Phone with an Online Camera Test

I'm standing in a café with a three-year-old phone listed at $185, and the question is simple: are both cameras healthy enough to pay full price? The seller has already shown me the gallery, but sample photos prove nothing about this unit today, so I open the test in the phone's own browser and allow access.

The back camera comes up first and reads 1600 × 1200, which works out to 1600 × 1200 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1.92 MP, with 146 frames in a 5-second sample, so 29.2 frames per second. Healthy. Then I switch to the front, and the readout drops to 640 × 480 at 14.2 frames per second (71 frames in 5 seconds, about 70 ms per frame). A 480-line short side falls below the 720 lines that the SMPTE 296M standard sets for 720p HD, so on paper the front side fails.

Before I walk away, I check the two things that fake this result. A messaging program with a video call minimised is still holding the front one, so I close it, reload and rerun:

Front sideFirst runRerun
Stream640 × 480 (0.31 MP)1280 × 960 (1.23 MP)
Frames in 5 s71146
Per second14.229.2
Time per frame70.4 ms34.2 ms

The rerun clears the 720-line threshold comfortably, and the frame time is now under the 41.7 ms needed to hold 24 frames per second. That reading of resolution and frames per second is what an online camera check is really for, and it says the front side is fine.

The part worth knowing: 640 × 480 is also what some browsers hand back when a page asks for no particular size, so a low first reading can come from the tool or another program rather than the camera. I'd never reject a phone on one run. Close background programs, rerun once, and only treat a result that stays under 720 lines as a real fault. Here it didn't, so I grab one frame from each side, see no dust spots, and pay the $185.

Camera Test Troubleshooting for a Black or Frozen Preview

A black screen or frozen frame almost always has one of four causes. Work through them in order.

Browser Permission Denied

If you blocked access earlier, open the site's permissions. In Chrome, tap the icon beside the address and set Camera to Allow. On iOS, use the page menu's website settings. The operating system has its own switch too, so make sure the browser app may use the camera in your phone's privacy settings.

Another App Is Holding the Camera

Only one program can use the camera at a time. Close the phone's own camera, Zoom, Skype or any background video chat, then reload. If the stream still will not start, restart the phone to release it.

Only One Camera Shows Up

Many phones hide ultra-wide and telephoto modules from web pages. Others list several back cameras; pick each in turn. If the switch control does nothing, the browser is the limit. Confirm it in the built-in camera before assuming it is dead.

Drivers, Codecs and Hardware Faults

  • On a computer, update the camera drivers and try another USB port or cable.
  • Make sure the browser supports the stream's codec.
  • On a mobile device, a camera that fails in every camera program even after a reboot is a hardware problem for repair.

Smartphone Camera vs Laptop Webcam Test Differences

The same page works on both, but a phone gives you more to check:

  • Lenses: a smartphone lets you switch between at least two cameras, while a webcam is usually a single fixed lens.
  • Resolution: phone streams often reach 1080p or more, while many built-in webcam modules stop at 720p.
  • Permissions: a phone asks once per site in the browser and again at system level, while a desktop webcam is often blocked by a privacy shutter or a system switch.
  • Autofocus: phone cameras refocus as you move, while most webcam optics are fixed and sharpest at one distance.

Running an Online Webcam Test on a Computer

On Windows or macOS, open the same page in a desktop browser. If the webcam shows a picture but calls still fail, test the microphone or speaker separately. A USB webcam should report its own name; a built-in webcam may be hidden behind a sliding cover.

iPhone, Android and Browser Support

Any current version of Chrome, Safari, Firefox or Edge supports the camera interface this online camera test relies on. On an iPhone, Safari and Chrome both work. On Android, Chrome, Firefox, Samsung Internet and Edge do. In-app viewers inside social apps are the usual exception; use a full browser instead.

When to Test Your Camera Before Relying on It

A two-minute check pays off whenever the camera must work first time.

Buying a Used Phone

Check both cameras before you pay: take a photo with each and look for dust under the glass, scratches, or a lens that will not sharpen. A quick camera check takes less time than a return.

Before Video Calls and Remote Work

If you join meetings from your phone for remote work, open the test a few minutes before a Google Meet session or any other video conferencing tool. It catches a blocked permission or a busy camera before everyone is waiting, and works the same for your laptop webcam.

Lab Benchmark Scores vs a Quick Phone Check

Lab reviews such as DXOMARK score a phone model across hundreds of controlled shots, showing how it compares when new. A browser test answers a narrower question: does this particular unit's camera work properly?

faq.question: How do I test my phone camera online?
faq.answer: Open the test in your phone's browser, tap Start and allow camera access. The live preview appears straight away, and you can switch between the front and rear cameras, read the resolution and frame rate, and capture a frame without installing an app.

faq.question: Can I test both the front and rear camera?
faq.answer: Yes, on phones that expose both to the browser. Use the switch control to move between them. If one never appears, the phone may only expose some of its cameras to web pages, so confirm it in the built-in camera app before assuming it is broken.

faq.question: Why is the resolution lower than my phone's megapixel rating?
faq.answer: The test reports the video stream the browser was given, not the sensor's rating. A 50 MP camera often streams around 2 to 3 MP, which is normal. Judge the number against video tiers such as 720p and 1080p instead.

faq.question: Why does my frame rate drop in a dark room?
faq.answer: In low light the camera uses a longer exposure for each frame, so fewer frames fit into a second. A camera that streams 30 frames per second in good light can fall well below that in dim conditions. Add light and test again.

faq.question: Can I use this as a webcam test on my laptop?
faq.answer: Yes. On a computer the same page opens your built-in or USB webcam and reports its resolution and frame rate, so you can check it before a video call.

faq.question: Why does the test show a black screen?
faq.answer: The usual causes are a blocked browser permission, the operating system's camera privacy switch, another app holding the camera, or a physical cover over the lens. Fix the permission, close other camera apps and reload the page.

faq.question: Is the camera test private?
faq.answer: Yes. The video is processed in your browser and never uploaded. Closing the tab stops the stream, and nothing is stored on a server.

content_html:
Can anyone actually hear you? A microphone test answers that in ten seconds: speak, watch the real-time meter move, then listen back on headphones before a call, podcast or streaming session. This online check gives you a clear pass or fail plus the audio readings behind it.

How to Test Your Microphone in Your Browser

On a laptop, desktop computer or smartphone, the browser microphone test runs locally with no software to install, a free online tool to open before any call:

  1. Click Start on the widget above.
  2. When the browser asks, click Allow so the page can use your mic.
  3. Pick your mic from the list if more than one appears.
  4. Speak a sentence at normal level and watch the meter.
  5. Record a short clip, then play it back.

Any recent version of Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Edge supports what this online mic test needs, on Windows, Android and iOS alike.

Allow Microphone Access and Choose the Input Device

Your browser blocks microphone access until you grant permission, and it remembers that choice per site. Click Block by mistake and the meter stays flat. Once access is granted, the device selector lists every mic the system can see: a headset, a webcam with a built-in microphone or the laptop's own array. With multiple microphones connected, the page may open on the default device, so pick the right entry first.

Read the Waveform and Visual Feedback

The moving waveform is the quickest way to check microphone function: if the sound waves jump when you speak and settle when you stop, the mic is live. A level meter (or visualizer bars) adds scale: normal speech should push the volume levels into the upper middle, well short of the top. A barely flickering trace means a switched-off or distant mic; one that hits the end on every word means the input is too hot.

Recording and Playback: Test My Mic by Ear

To hear what other people hear, record a 10-second clip and play it back. Use headphones for live monitoring, because routing your mic to your speakers creates a feedback loop. Listen for hum, a hollow room sound, or words that break up. You can download the audio clip as an MP3 or a lossless WAV; browser recordings are usually mono with a 16 bit depth, plenty for a voice check.

What the Microphone Test Tool Reports About Your Mic

A good tester also reads the settings your browser negotiated with the mic. Here's a sample report from a desk mic during a test recording. Running the microphone test online keeps the data on your machine, with nothing sent to a server, which matters for privacy.

ReadingExample valueWhat it tells you
Sample rate48,000 HzHow many snapshots are taken each second
Sample size16 bitsHow finely each snapshot is measured
Audio channels1One channel, normal for speech
Echo cancellationOnRemoves far-end audio leaking back in
Noise suppressionOnFilters steady hum and fan sounds
Automatic gain controlOnRaises or lowers your level for you
Buffer delay21.3 msTime before your speech reaches the page
Peak level−9.0 dBFSLoudest moment of the test sentence

What the Format Readings Mean

The sample rate sets the highest pitch the mic can capture, half the rate: 48,000 Hz covers up to 24 kHz, past the 20Hz–20kHz range of human hearing. Sample size sets how finely each snapshot is measured; 16 bits is the norm for calls and 24 bits for studio recording. Audio channels reads 1 for almost any speech mic.

What the Processing Flags Do

Your browser applies three filters by default. Echo cancellation strips sound from your own speakers out of the mic feed, so the other side doesn't hear itself repeated. Noise suppression removes steady sounds such as fans and air conditioning. Automatic gain control rides your level up and down. All three help two-way communication but colour a clip, so if yours sounds pumping or underwater, these filters are the first suspect; switch them off in the recording app.

Input Level, Latency and Signal-to-Noise Ratio

Levels are read in dBFS (decibels relative to full scale), where 0 is the ceiling:

$$\text{dBFS} = 20 \log_{10}(A)$$

Here \(A\) is the sample amplitude, from 0 to 1. In the sample report, a speaking peak of \(A = 0.355\) gives −9.0 dBFS, and the quiet gap between words sits at \(A = 0.00089\), or −61.0 dBFS. The signal-to-noise ratio is the difference between the two:

$$\text{SNR} = -9.0 - (-61.0) = 52\ \text{dB}$$

A gap that wide keeps hiss and room tone far beneath your voice; part of that quiet floor is the mic's own self-noise. Peaks between roughly −18 and −6 dBFS leave headroom, while anything touching 0 dBFS causes clipping, a hard distortion no filter can undo.

Delay follows its own formula:

$$\text{latency} = \frac{\text{buffer size}}{\text{samples per second}} = \frac{1024}{48{,}000} = 21.3\ \text{ms}$$

Under about 30 ms, you won't notice the lag while monitoring yourself.

A Microphone Check Before a Remote Job Interview

A job candidate has a panel interview on Microsoft Teams in 40 minutes and one decision to make: speak through her laptop's built-in mic, or dig out the wired headset from a drawer. She runs both through the mic check and reads the numbers rather than trusting her ears. The answer comes back clearly: the headset wins, with a 47.8 dB gap between speech and the quiet floor against the laptop's 25.7 dB.

She starts with the laptop, sitting at her usual 35 cm from the screen, and reads her opening line ("I've spent six years in supply-chain analytics") twice. The peak amplitude settles at 0.081, which is \(20 \log_{10}(0.081)\) = −21.8 dBFS, below the −18 dBFS alignment level that EBU R 68 uses as a broadcast reference. The pause between sentences sits at 0.0042, or −47.5 dBFS, mostly the laptop's own fan.

Then she plugs in the headset, its boom about 4 cm from the corner of her mouth, and repeats the same line:

SetupSpeech peakQuiet floorGap
Laptop mic, fan running−21.8 dBFS−47.5 dBFS25.7 dB
Laptop mic, fan throttled−21.8 dBFS−54.4 dBFS32.6 dB
Wired headset, 4 cm−11.4 dBFS−59.2 dBFS47.8 dB

She checks the middle row on purpose: closing a browser tab full of video drops the fan, and the floor falls 6.9 dB. That helps, but the laptop still loses by 15.2 dB, so the fan was never the main problem. Distance was.

What I'd flag here is the gap between theory and the reading. Going from 35 cm to 4 cm should add \(20 \log_{10}(35 \div 4)\) = 18.8 dB, yet her peak only rose 10.4 dB. The laptop's automatic gain control had already boosted her quiet speech before the meter saw it, which flatters the laptop's peak and lifts its floor at the same time. That's why the test's peak reading on its own can mislead you: with gain riding, compare the gap between the meter's two readings, not the loudest moment, and read it after the first two or three seconds once the gain has settled.

Her next step is concrete: headset in, Teams input switched to it by name rather than "Default", and one 15-second recording played back to confirm the −11.4 dBFS peak isn't clipping on louder words. If the interview runs long and she has to move to the laptop, she now knows to lean in to about 20 cm and kill the video tab first.

Microphone Not Working? Fixes After a Microphone Check

When the meter stays flat, the usual culprit isn't the mic at all: Zoom, Discord, Microsoft Teams or Google Meet can hold exclusive control, so close those apps first. Then follow this troubleshooting order and test your microphone again after each fix.

Browser Permission and Privacy Settings

In Chrome, click the icon left of the address bar and set the mic to Allow; in Firefox, clear the block in the same panel. The operating system can still block it: Windows and macOS privacy settings decide which apps may use the mic, overriding anything you allow in the page. On Linux, check the input source in your sound server.

Sound Settings, Input Volume and Device Manager

  • On Windows 11, open Settings, then System, then Sound, and pick the mic under Input.
  • On a Mac, open System Settings, then Sound, then Input.
  • Make sure the mic isn't muted and the slider isn't near zero: a mic at 5% passes but sounds distant.
  • Check for a physical mute button, often on the cord.
  • If the mic doesn't show up, open Device Manager, update or reinstall the audio drivers, then restart; on a Mac, restarting Core Audio clears a stuck input.

Cable, USB Port and Hardware Failure Checks

Reseat the plug, try a different USB port or swap in a second audio jack lead. Crackle or static that changes when you move the cable points to a damaged lead. Bluetooth headsets drop to a low-quality call mode while the mic is active, so test wired if you can. If it fails on a second computer too, the unit is faulty.

Types of Microphone Testing for Better Sound Quality

These checks test microphone performance, not just function. Run them in a quiet environment, twice each, and open clips in Audacity or other recording software that shows a spectrum.

Background Noise and Frequency Response Tests

Record ten seconds of silence, then ten of speech, and compare. The silent part reveals background noise (fans, traffic, keyboard clicks) and the ambient noise of a bare room. Room acoustics matter as much as the mic: soft furnishings cut the reflections that make speech sound hollow. Frequency response describes which pitches a mic favours; a speech mic often lifts the upper mids for clarity, which you hear on playback.

Distance and Polar Pattern Tests

Your level changes with distance by the inverse-square rule:

$$\Delta L = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)$$

To run it with the test, record the same line at 25 cm and then at 8 cm: the peak dBFS reading should rise by about \(20 \log_{10}(25 \div 8)\) = +9.9 dB, and that close you'll also hear the proximity effect, a bass boost. Keep a consistent distance once the meter peaks in the target band, and use a pop filter to tame plosives. To check the polar pattern, watch the meter as you talk from the front, side and behind: a cardioid mic's peak drops sharply at the back; an omnidirectional one reads the same all round.

Why Use a Mic Test Tool Before Meetings

A ten-second check before meetings, video calls or a webinar spares you the "can you hear me?" minute at the start, and it catches the wrong input before a podcast recording you can't redo. Whenever you check mic levels on a new setup, test your mic again after every change.

Choosing a USB or XLR Microphone for Better Audio Quality

If the test exposes a weak mic, a USB mic plugs straight in and is the easy route for content creation. An XLR mic needs an audio interface (and phantom power for a condenser) but gives more control. Let the test results pick the type: if your silent recording showed a high floor, dynamic mics reject more room sound and handle high SPL; if your clip sounded dull, condensers have higher sensitivity and catch more detail. For a home office, a dynamic model is often the better audio quality pick.

faq.question: Is my audio sent anywhere during the mic test?
faq.answer: No. The test runs in your browser, and any clip you record stays on your device unless you download and share it yourself.

faq.question: Do I need to install software to test my microphone?
faq.answer: No. A recent version of Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Edge is enough. You only have to allow microphone access when the browser asks.

faq.question: Can I test a microphone on my phone?
faq.answer: Yes. Mobile browsers on Android and iOS support the test. Keep the page in the foreground and don't lock the screen, or the browser may pause the mic.

faq.question: Why is my recording too quiet or too loud?
faq.answer: Your input level is set too low or too high. Adjust it in your system sound settings, keep a steady distance from the mic, and aim for peaks between -18 and -6 dBFS.

faq.question: Why do I hear an echo during the test?
faq.answer: Your speakers are feeding sound back into the mic. Use headphones when you listen to yourself, and keep echo cancellation switched on for calls.

faq.question: How do I test my mic on Windows 11?
faq.answer: Open Settings, then System, then Sound, choose your microphone under Input and speak; the input volume bar should move as you talk.

faq.question: Why does the test say my microphone is in use or blocked?
faq.answer: Another app such as Zoom, Teams or Discord may be holding the mic, or the browser or operating system has blocked access. Close the other app, then check the site permission and your privacy settings.

content_html:
Not sure both of your speakers work, or that the left speaker and right speaker are wired the right way round? Play the online speaker test tones on this page and you'll know in seconds which side each tone lands on, how low and high your system reaches, and whether it is wired correctly. It runs in your browser, with no download and no app.

How the Online Sound Test Works in Your Browser

Each button sends a short signal to your audio output, so a passing sound test proves the whole chain works: browser, operating system and speaker hardware. It works on a computer or phone, and nothing is recorded.

  1. Click Left, then Right, and note where each tone comes from.
  2. Play the rising tone and note where the tone appears and fades.
  3. Play the polarity pair and compare the low end.

Web Audio API and the Test Tone

The Web Audio API built into modern browsers generates each test tone live. Some pages add a visualizer, a waveform like an oscilloscope trace, but it shows the signal leaving the page, not what your speakers reproduce.

Stereo Test for Left and Right Channels

A stereo test plays a tone on one side at a time. Stereophonic sound depends on the left and right channels staying separate; if Left plays from your right, the stereo imaging of every film is mirrored. The centred tone checks stereo balance on speakers or headphones.

ToneYou should hearA fault sounds like
Left / RightOne side onlyBoth sides, or the wrong side
CentreA tone in the middlePulled to one side (poor channel balance)
Polarity pairA focused toneWide and thin in both versions
Rising toneA smooth climb in pitchDead spots, rattling or buzzing

Stereo Sound Test for Swapped or One-Sided Sound

If one side stays silent, check the cable linking the two speakers, and that you're in the green jack on a desktop PC; a worn 3.5mm jack can also make playback one-sided. If the sides are swapped, swap the speaker wires or fix the wiring at the amplifier, so your audio channels stay labelled correctly.

Frequency Sweep and Bass Speaker Tests

A frequency sweep glides one tone from the lowest to the highest pitch. Most climb logarithmically, the same number of octaves each second, so you can turn the moment a tone appears or vanishes into a frequency:

$$f(t) = f_{0} \times \left(\frac{f_{1}}{f_{0}}\right)^{t/T}$$

Here \(f_{0}\) is the start, \(f_{1}\) the end, \(t\) the seconds elapsed and \(T\) the run length, in hertz (Hz) and seconds. Say a 16-second run climbs from 20Hz to 20kHz and you're checking a 13-inch laptop. The rumble becomes audible at 4.5 seconds, about 140Hz, and the tone fades at 15.1 seconds, about 13.6 kHz. It passes 440Hz at 7.2 seconds and 1000Hz at 9.1 seconds. Each second covers roughly 0.62 octaves, so a half-second timing slip shifts the answer by a third of an octave.

Frequency Response From 20Hz to 20kHz

Frequency response is the range a speaker reproduces and how evenly. Laptop speakers lose the bottom few hundred Hz; a sudden drop in level often marks the crossover between woofer and tweeter, and distortion, crackles or a hum at one pitch usually mean resonance in the speaker cabinet. Treble vanishing early isn't always the speaker: if headphones fade at the same second of the run, the limit is age-related hearing loss at the top of your hearing range, so take a hearing test before blaming your audio equipment.

Bass Test and Treble Test Limits

A bass test holds low frequencies, often 100Hz and below, to check a subwoofer for rattle; a treble test plays high frequencies to catch hiss. A mono test sends identical sound to both sides to show whether one driver is weaker. If the low end sounds muffled, check that an equalizer preset or bass boost hasn't been switched off, then compare with music you know.

Speaker Polarity Test With Test Tones

Speaker polarity is about wiring. Each cable has a positive and a negative lead; reverse one pair and the cones move in opposite directions. A polarity test plays one low tone twice: in phase, then with one side inverted.

In Phase vs Out of Phase

Sit in a triangle formation with both speakers, since good speaker placement makes the difference easy to hear. The normal version should feel solid; the out of phase version sounds wide and hollow because the sound waves partly cancel in the room. If the inverted one sounds fuller, a speaker is wired backwards; swap the red and black leads on one side.

Matching a Desk Subwoofer Crossover With an Online Speaker Test

I'm wiring a pair of second-hand passive bookshelf speakers to a small amplifier, with an 8-inch subwoofer under the desk. The question is simple: where should the subwoofer's crossover dial sit so nothing goes missing between the sub and the bookshelves? The answer turned out to be 100Hz, not the 80Hz the dial shipped at, because these speakers only start playing at about 92Hz. The left/right, polarity and rising tones on this page are how I measure that.

The order matters. Left and Right land on the correct sides first time. Then the polarity pair: the inverted version sounds fuller than the normal one, which means one speaker is wired backwards. I swap the red and black leads on the right speaker and replay; now the normal version is the solid one. I do this before measuring anything else, because reversed polarity cancels low notes between the speakers and would push the starting point of the next check higher than it really is.

With the sub switched off, I play a 24-second logarithmic sweep from 20Hz to 20kHz and watch a stopwatch. A clear rumble arrives at 5.3 seconds. Plugging that into the formula: 20 × 10005.3/24 ≈ 92Hz. I cross-check with a steady tone from the tone generator: 90Hz is faint but present, 80Hz is barely there. Since my stopwatch thumb is the weak link, I solve for the times either side:

Rumble heard atFrequency
5.0 s84Hz
5.3 s92Hz
5.6 s100Hz

Measured against the 80Hz crossover THX recommends for home systems, that leaves a gap between 80Hz and about 92Hz where neither box carries the note. Even the late end of my timing range lands at 100Hz, so I set the dial there and rerun the sweep with the sub on: the rumble now starts almost immediately and stays even through the handover, which confirms the gap is closed.

One caveat a spec sheet won't give you: at a desk, room reflections can cancel a single low note at your head. I moved back 40cm and repeated the run; the start moved by only 0.2 seconds, so this was the speakers, not the room. Had it jumped by half a second or more, I'd trust the room, not the speaker, and fix seating before touching the dial. The input I'd watch most is that start time, since each second here spans only 0.42 octaves.

Tone Generator, Sine Wave and Noise in a Sound Tester

A tone generator plays a steady pitch you choose, such as 440Hz (concert A) or 1000Hz, to find one buzzing panel or match two speakers. A spectrum analyzer paired with a microphone shows which frequencies your speakers actually put out during a tone, capped by its sample rate: a capture taken 48,000 times a second stops at 24 kHz.

White Noise vs Pink Noise

The white kind spreads equal energy across every hertz and sounds like bright hiss. Pink noise puts equal energy in each octave, closer to how your ears judge loudness, so installers use it to calibrate a system and some owners play it for speaker burn-in.

Phone Speaker Test Online for iPhone, Android and Earbuds

On an iPhone or Android handset, expect a thin low end and treat a phone speaker as mono unless the model has stereo drivers. Tones follow the system output, so a paired Bluetooth headset, earbuds or AirPods take over. Check speech clarity across the voice range: a muffled voice on calls can be the microphone, so run a microphone test too. Two-channel tones can't check 5.1 surround sound.

Headphone Test and Speaker Cleaning

A headphone test uses the same left/right logic at lower levels. If a phone speaker sounds distorted after getting wet, a speaker cleaning tone vibrates water out of the grille; replay the tones to confirm the fix.

Audio Check When You Hear No Sound

Work through this audio check from the quickest fix to the most involved.

Volume, Output Device and Safe Levels

  • Pick the right output device, or playback device, in sound settings on Windows or macOS; HDMI monitors often grab it.
  • Check the speakers are powered on and no mute key is active.
  • Start at a low volume, about a quarter of maximum, and raise it slowly.

Audio Driver and Sound Card Fixes

If nothing plays anywhere on the computer, update the audio driver from your sound card or motherboard maker and restart. Faulty hardware is the last suspect, not the first.

When the Audio Test Passes but an App Stays Silent

If this audio test plays but Zoom or YouTube stays quiet, your audio gear is fine and the problem is software. Check the volume mixer on Windows or per-app volume on a Mac, the tab's speaker icon and the app's output choice, and close programs holding the device. A pass here only proves the browser path; it can't see settings inside other apps.

faq.question: What can I use this tone generator for?
faq.answer: This tool lets you generate pure audio tones to test speakers and headphones for stereo balance, phase issues, and resonant frequencies. It's also useful for tuning instruments to a reference pitch, testing your hearing sensitivity across frequencies, and diagnosing audio equipment problems.

faq.question: What's the difference between a Speaker Test and a Headphone Test?
faq.answer: A speaker test checks your room's acoustic environment along with the speaker's stereo balance and frequency response. A headphone test focuses on left/right channel isolation and in-ear frequency accuracy. Use the channel selector in this tool to isolate left or right output for either test type.

faq.question: What is the safe volume level to use?
faq.answer: Start with a comfortable volume at a reference frequency like 1,000 Hz and avoid increasing it significantly when testing other frequencies — especially high ones where your hearing is most vulnerable. Prolonged exposure to loud tones, even if you can barely hear them, can damage hearing and equipment.

faq.question: Why is the resonant frequency of a speaker important?
faq.answer: Every speaker has a resonant frequency (Fs) at which it vibrates most efficiently. Playing a tone at this frequency helps you identify the speaker's natural resonance point. Knowing this is essential for subwoofer box design, enclosure tuning, and ensuring your speaker isn't being driven outside its optimal range.

faq.question: How do I find the resonant frequency of my speaker?
faq.answer: Start at a low frequency (around 20–40 Hz for subwoofers) and slowly sweep upward. The resonant frequency is where the cone excursion (movement) is greatest and you may notice a change in perceived loudness. This corresponds to the Thiele/Small parameter Fs.

faq.question: What are the different waveform types and when should I use them?
faq.answer: Sine waves are pure tones with no harmonics — ideal for precise frequency testing. Square waves contain strong odd harmonics and stress tweeters more. Sawtooth waves have the richest harmonic content and are good for full-range speaker stress tests. Triangle waves are smoother than square waves and useful for mid-range checks.

faq.question: Are the test results accurate?
faq.answer: The tone is generated using the Web Audio API at a sample rate of 44.1 kHz, which ensures excellent accuracy across the audible spectrum. However, actual sound output quality depends on your device's audio hardware, drivers, and speaker/headphone quality.

faq.question: Can I use this speaker test on mobile?
faq.answer: Yes. The tool runs entirely in your browser using the Web Audio API and is compatible with modern versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge on both desktop and mobile. Make sure your device's volume is set to a safe level before playing any tones.

subtitle: Click Measure Now on this webcam fps test to get your camera's real Measured FPS.

Your camera feed will appear here

—Requested FPS
—Measured FPS
—Frame Rate Range
—Method Used

Requested FPS comes from getSettings() — what your browser negotiated with the camera, not what it delivers frame-by-frame. Measured FPS counts real delivered frames over the run.

Status & Per-Second Frame Rate

What to do if the camera won't start, plus a bar chart of frames delivered each second of the last run
