h1: Webcam Comparison: View Two Cameras Side by Side Live
subtitle: Pick two cameras and click Start Comparison on this webcam comparison tool to view both feeds side by side.

card.fields_html:
Side-by-Side Camera Comparison

Compare a laptop camera against an external webcam, or any two connected cameras, directly

Camera A
Camera A will appear here
Camera B
Camera B will appear here
Pick two cameras above (or leave on Default) and click Start Comparison.

content_html:
Your laptop camera might look fine on its own, but you only find out how good it is when you put it next to another one. The side-by-side camera comparison is a webcam comparison that runs two webcams live in the same browser tab, so you see both feeds against the same lamp, the same background and the same face at the same moment. That turns a vague hunch about your video calls into a clear answer: which one looks better in your home office, and by how much.

How the Side-by-Side Camera Comparison Works

The tool asks your browser for access, lists every connected video device, and opens two live previews next to each other. Nothing is uploaded: both streams stay on your computer, and the only file the tool ever creates is the comparison image you choose to download.

Choosing Camera A and Camera B

Pick one device from the Camera A menu and another from Camera B, then click Start Comparison. If two are plugged in, the tool selects different ones by default. A built-in camera usually appears under a generic name, while a webcam shows its model name once you allow access. Plug an external model straight into the computer rather than a crowded hub, ideally a USB 3.0 port, so it doesn't drop frames while both feeds run. The browser reads devices the same way on Windows and macOS, so no extra driver or software is needed, and any image settings you changed in the maker's own app still apply here.

Swap, Split and Download the Comparison

Once both feeds are live, Swap A ↔ B moves each one to the other half of the screen, which helps you check that you aren't simply preferring whichever image sits on the left. Vertical Split stacks the feeds one above the other, handy on a narrow monitor or a phone. Download Comparison saves both frames as one image, more reliable than juggling two separate screenshots when you want to show a colleague or revisit the result later.

When Only One Camera Can Run at a Time

Some phones, tablets and older drivers can't open two video devices at once. When that happens, the tool switches to capture mode: you take a still from A, then one from B, and the two stills appear next to each other. Each live preview is also requested at a moderate 640 × 480, because two streams roughly double the bandwidth and processor load. Judge color, exposure and framing here, and leave fine-detail checks to each webcam's full-resolution recording.

Built-In Webcam or External Webcam: Who Needs a Comparison

Most people reach for this test when they're unsure whether a purchase is worth the price, or whether a new webcam actually beat the old one.

When Your Laptop Camera Is Good Enough

Recent premium laptops, such as a current MacBook, now ship cameras that hold up well in everyday video meetings. If your built-in webcam already renders your face cleanly next to a borrowed webcam, an upgrade buys little. Many cheaper and older machines, though, still use small 720p modules whose image quality turns soft and muddy as soon as daylight fades. Running the comparison before you spend anything tells you which group your computer belongs to.

Reasons to Add a Dedicated Webcam

A dedicated webcam makes sense if you work from a desktop computer with no camera, if your built-in lens sits at an unflattering angle under the screen, or if you spend hours a day working from home on calls where people notice picture quality. The comparison is also the quickest way to check that an external webcam you just bought is genuinely better, not just newer. One thing to note while it runs is eyeline: a webcam mounted high on a tall stand can make you look as if you're glancing away, which matters more for remote work than a slight gain in detail.

How to Compare the Images Fairly

A fair test changes one thing only: the device. Everything else, from the light to the app, has to stay the same while you compare the images.

Match the Lighting Conditions First

Run the comparison at least three times under different lighting conditions: soft natural light from the front, a backlit scene with bright daylight behind you, and an evening scene lit only by a desk lamp. The bright-background case separates good webcams from weak ones fastest, because each has to balance a glowing background against a darker face. Keep both the same distance from you and point them at the same spot, otherwise one gets an easier shot.

Rank the Results With a Blind Panel

Your own bias is the biggest risk in any comparison. Download the comparison image from each setup, hide which feed is which, and ask two or three people to rank them. A small panel like this is how professional reviewers test webcams, and it works just as well at home. For audio and motion, also save short recordings of yourself reading the same paragraph in front of each one.

Test Inside Zoom, Teams and OBS

Your browser shows each device's own output, but video conferencing apps compress it again. After the browser check, open the winner in Zoom, Microsoft Teams or Discord and confirm it still looks better there. If you plan on streaming or making presentations, test in OBS as well, both full screen and scaled down to a small face-cam window, since streaming software applies its own scaling and sharpening.

What to Check When You Compare Them Directly

When both feeds are on screen, it's tempting to pick whichever looks brighter. Instead, compare them directly one quality at a time, using the checks below.

Image Quality, Sharpness and Low Light Noise

Overall image quality comes down mostly to the sensor and the lens aperture. Look at fine detail such as hair, fabric and text on a mug: real detail shows crisp edges, while heavy processing paints them on. Then dim the room. Small sensors produce visible noise in the dark, a grainy crawl in shadows and blotchy color. Larger ones, such as the 1/1.3-inch sensor in some premium models, and features like dual native ISO keep the picture clean much longer, which is why a bigger sensor improves image quality more than extra pixels do.

White Balance and Skin Tones

White balance decides where the webcam sets its white point for the light in your room. Get it wrong and the whole picture takes on a blue or yellow tint. Hold a sheet of white paper next to your face: in a color-accurate feed it stays white and your face looks natural-looking rather than orange or grey. Watch how fast auto white balance settles after you switch a lamp on, too. Color accuracy matters more than resolution for most calls, because poor color quality is noticed by everyone, while missing detail rarely is. If one feed needs manual color correction in its software to match the other, count that against it.

Exposure, Contrast and HDR

Exposure is how bright the image is overall, contrast is the gap between dark and light, and saturation is how intense the colors are. In the bright-background test, a weak webcam's auto exposure either leaves your face in shadow or turns the background white and overexposed. Models with HDR handle this far better, though some drop to a lower frame rate while it's on. Check the corners too: a strong vignette darkens the edges, and too much brightness washes everything out.

Autofocus and Focus Speed

Lean toward each lens, then hold an object up close. Good autofocus locks on within a second, and focus speed is where cheap webcams show themselves by hunting back and forth. A fixed focus model never hunts, but anything closer than arm's length stays soft. Some webcams add a Show Mode that snaps focus to an object you present, while larger sensors give a little natural bokeh, a soft background blur without any software effect.

Resolution and Frame Rate on a Standalone Webcam

Every standalone webcam box leads with two numbers, resolution and frame rate, and both are worth checking against the full specifications once your comparison result is in.

720p, 1080p, 2K or a 4K Webcam

Resolution is the pixel count of each frame. The lowest common step is standard HD (about 0.9 megapixel), 1080p is Full HD (2.1 megapixels, 2.25 times as many), 2K or 1440p is 3.7 megapixels, and Ultra HD 4K resolution reaches 8.3 megapixels, four times 1080p. A 4K webcam lets you crop and zoom without losing detail, but call apps usually send 720p or 1080p anyway, so for most people 1080p is the sweet spot. Read the specs with care: a spec sheet that lists 4K at 30 frames may only manage 1080p at the higher rate.

  • Standard HD: fine for casual calls with good light
  • 1080p: the right baseline resolution for daily work calls
  • 2K: a little extra detail for cropping
  • 4K: useful for recording YouTube videos, not needed for most meetings

Frame Rate and Frames Per Second

Frame rate is measured in frames per second. 30 fps is standard for calls; 60 fps makes movement smoother, which streamers and anyone who gestures a lot will notice. Higher settings also use more of your internet connection, so a webcam that sends 4K at 60 fps can stutter on a busy home network while 1080p plays smoothly. The field of view (FOV) sits on the same line of the specifications: around 65 to 80 degrees frames one person at a desk, while 90 degrees and wider shows more of your room than you may want. A wide field of view also makes your face smaller at the same resolution. Of these, field of view is the one the live comparison shows straight away: frame both feeds on the same chair and the wider one puts more wall around you. Smoothness at 60 fps can't show in the 640 × 480 preview, so check it in each webcam's own footage or in its software preview. Overall video quality depends on all three numbers plus the lens, so treat the spec sheet as a starting point and your own comparison as the final word.

Worked Example: A Laptop Camera Against a USB Webcam

Here is how one comparison plays out. Camera A is the 720p module built into a four-year-old laptop. Camera B is a 1080p USB webcam clipped to the top of an external monitor. Both are scored from 1 to 5 on six checks, with the comparison image downloaded in every light setup and ranked blind by two other people.

CheckA: built-inB: USB
Fine detail24
White balance and skin tones34
Exposure with a backlit window24
Low light noise13
Autofocus34
Framing and eyeline43
Total (out of 30)1522

B wins by 7 points out of 30, roughly 50% against 73%. The gap isn't spread evenly, though. Averaged across all six checks, the two score 3.2 and 4.0 in soft daylight, a gap of only 0.8. With bright daylight behind the desk, they score 1.8 and 3.3, and under the evening lamp, 1.5 and 2.8. The USB model earns most of its lead in hard light, so someone who only takes calls at midday facing the light gains far less than someone who works into the evening.

The one check A wins, framing, is worth noticing too. The built-in lens sits closer to the person's eye level on screen, while the webcam on the taller monitor looks slightly down. Lowering it a few centimetres fixes that, which shows why the comparison is worth re-running after you adjust the setup, not just once.

How I Test Webcams Before the Return Window Closes

I tutor online from 6 to 9 pm, and I have 11 days left to return a 2K webcam that cost me $84.99. The question is simple: does it beat the 1080p pop-up camera built into my monitor enough to keep? It doesn't: the lead is 3 points out of 30, and a $29 lamp cuts it to 2.

At 6:50 pm, under the 2700K ceiling light I actually teach in, I set the monitor camera as Camera A and the webcam as Camera B, sit 64 cm back, and click Start Comparison. I wait about five seconds before downloading, because both feeds visibly brighten as their auto exposure settles. I download four comparison images, swapping A and B between them, and my partner ranks them without knowing which is which. B wins three of the four.

Scoring the same six checks as above gives A 17 and B 20. Then I rerun it with one change: a 5600K LED panel at 45 degrees to my left.

SetupA: monitorB: 2K webcamGap
Ceiling light only17203
Ceiling light + LED panel21232

The lamp adds 4 points to A and 3 to B, so the light improves my picture more than the camera swap does. I cross-check the one thing the side-by-side camera comparison can't show: detail. The preview runs at 640 × 480, so the 2K sensor's extra pixels are invisible here, and they'd mostly be invisible to students too. My upload speed test reads 4.3 Mbps, and Zoom lists 3.8 Mbps upload for 1080p group video, which leaves no room to send anything sharper even if the app allowed it.

One caveat I'd flag: if your device falls back to capture mode, the still is grabbed a moment after the stream opens, before exposure settles. Take each capture twice and keep the second.

The number to watch is the gap, not the totals. A 2-point lead in a light I'll actually use doesn't justify $84.99 plus a monitor clip that blocks my speaker grille, so the webcam goes back and the LED panel stays.

Tracking, Mics and Mounts: Comparing Products Beyond the Picture

Once picture quality is settled, the remaining differences come down to features and price. When comparing products, check these against the way you actually work.

Subject Tracking, Pan and Tilt

Subject tracking keeps you in frame as you move. Cheaper webcams do it with digital zoom, cropping into a wide shot, which costs detail. Premium models mount the lens on a motorized gimbal that physically turns to pan and tilt after you, guided by AI tracking. In the live comparison, walk across the room and watch both feeds: good face tracking moves smoothly, while poor auto-framing jumps and zooms in and out. A gimbal unit also stands taller than a flat webcam, which affects where your eyes appear to point.

Built-In Microphone and Audio Quality

The tool compares video only, so compare sound the same way you ranked the pictures: record the same paragraph through each webcam's mic, then play the two clips back to back next to the comparison image. The average webcam mic is no better than a laptop's, and several popular models skip the built-in microphone entirely. The better ones use a noise-cancelling array, which you'll hear as less fan hum on one clip than the other. If neither clip sounds clear, a USB mic or a headset usually beats any webcam mic, often for a lower price than a premium webcam.

Privacy Shutter, Mounts and Cables

Mounts decide whether a comparison is fair. Set both webcams at the same height and distance: a monitor mount that grips firmly keeps one from drooping halfway through the test, and a tripod mount lets you put it on a tripod level with the other one. Plug each one straight into the computer; a detachable USB-C cable has to reach from the top of your screen, and a USB-C to USB-A adapter covers older ports. Once the comparison is done, a built-in privacy shutter is the feature worth preferring between two close results, since a stick-on privacy cover is easy to lose.

Choosing a Face Cam on a Budget

A good face cam doesn't have to carry a high price. The comparison tool helps here, because you can test a cheap model against your current one before the return window closes.

Budget Picks Versus Upgrade Picks

Budget webcams usually offer 1080p at 30 fps, fixed or slow autofocus, and basic software. Upgrade picks add a larger sensor, HDR, tracking and better mics, often at two or three times the price. In the live comparison, a budget pick should clearly beat an older built-in module on the dim-room and bright-background checks; an upgrade pick only earns its higher price if it then beats the budget pick on those same checks by more than a point or two. Confirm compatibility and plug and play support first, because a webcam that needs the maker's software (or its firmware updates) before it shows up in your browser can't be compared at all. Your own comparison result is a better guide to picture quality than any price tag.

Fix the Lighting Before You Spend More

Light often matters more than the hardware. In the worked example, the cheap built-in module's daylight score came within 0.8 of the USB model, so a soft light in front of you can close much of the gap for nothing. Basic photography rules apply: light your face from the front, keep bright glass out of the background, and raise the lens to eye level for a flattering image. Content creators who stream on Twitch or need clean footage for recording should add a key light first, then run the comparison again before deciding whether a pricier webcam is still worth it.

faq.question: How do I compare two webcams at the same time?
faq.answer: Connect both cameras, pick one as Camera A and the other as Camera B, then start the comparison. Both feeds play live next to each other, so you see them under the same light at the same moment. Swap them once to check you aren't just favouring the left-hand image.

faq.question: Why does only one camera work on my phone or tablet?
faq.answer: Many phones, tablets and older drivers can open only one camera at a time. The tool then switches to capture mode: you take a still from each camera in turn and the two stills are shown together instead.

faq.question: Which is better for video calls, a 4K or a 1080p webcam?
faq.answer: For most calls, 1080p is enough. Zoom, Teams and Google Meet usually send 720p or 1080p, so a 4K webcam's extra detail is mostly useful for recording or cropping. Lighting, white balance and low-light noise make a bigger difference you can see in a side-by-side comparison.

faq.question: Do I need an external webcam if my laptop already has one?
faq.answer: Not always. Recent premium laptops have decent cameras, but many cheaper or older ones still use small 720p sensors that struggle in dim or backlit rooms. Compare your built-in camera with a webcam in the light you actually use before you buy.

faq.question: Is a built-in microphone important in a webcam?
faq.answer: It helps, but most webcam microphones sound no better than a laptop's, and some models have none at all. If clear speech matters, a USB microphone or a headset usually sounds better. Record the same sentence through each option and play them back to back.

faq.question: What should I look for when comparing two webcams?
faq.answer: Check one quality at a time: fine detail, white balance and skin tones, exposure with a bright window behind you, noise in low light, autofocus speed, and framing. Image quality depends more on the sensor and lighting than on the resolution printed on the box.

faq.question: Can I use my phone as one of the cameras?
faq.answer: Yes, if your computer sees it as a webcam. Apps that turn a phone into a webcam make it show up as a normal video device, so you can pick it as Camera A or B and compare it with your laptop camera.

h1: Webcam Focus Test & Sharpness Webcam Test: Test Your Webcam
subtitle: Click Start Camera to run this webcam focus test and watch your Score climb as you sharpen the shot.

card.fields_html:
Sharpness & Focus Test

Point the camera at something with fine detail — text, a patterned fabric, a bookshelf — and adjust focus while watching the meter

Your camera feed will appear here
Sharpness—
BlurrySoftSharpVery Sharp
Click Start Camera and allow access when your browser asks.

Live Reading

Updates a few times a second

—Score (0–100)
—Best This Session

The score is relative, not absolute — a blank wall scores low regardless of focus. Point the camera at something with visible detail and watch the score respond as you adjust focus; the response is the real test, not the raw number.

Printable Focus Chart

A generated test chart for manual focus verification

Print it or display it on a second screen, then check whether the fine spokes near the centre stay distinct at your camera's normal working distance.

content_html:
Your face looks fine on your own screen, yet colleagues keep saying you look soft. The Sharpness and Focus Test measures that for you: it reads the edges in your webcam feed, turns them into a focus score from 0 to 100, and tells you whether the picture is sharp, slightly soft or blurry. It also watches noise levels, so grain can't pass as crisp. Use this webcam focus test to test your camera before an interview, a class or a streaming session, and see your image sharpness as a number rather than a guess.

How the Sharpness and Focus Test Scores Your Webcam

A sharp picture has hard edges; a blurred one smears them across several pixels. This webcam testing tool measures that in real time, on a square crop in the middle of the frame, and compares each frame with the sharpest frame the test has seen in this session:

$$S = 100 \times \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\nabla^2 I)}{\operatorname{Var}_{\text{peak}}(\nabla^2 I)}}$$

Here \(\nabla^2 I\) is the Laplacian of the frame, \(\operatorname{Var}\) is its variance across the crop, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\text{peak}}\) is the highest variance recorded so far. The square root turns variance back into a contour-strength scale, so a score of 50 means the edges are about half as strong as at the peak.

Laplacian Variance and the Live Preview

The Laplacian adds up the four neighbours of each pixel and subtracts four times the pixel itself. On a flat wall the result is near zero; on a crisp outline it swings far positive and negative. High variance means many strong outlines, which is what fine details such as eyelashes and printed text produce. While you watch the live preview, the browser repeats this on every frame. That is also how contrast-detect focusing works inside many webcams: the optics move until local contrast peaks. Grab a snapshot in the browser to compare a frozen frame with its score.

What the Score Bands Mean for Video Calls

ScoreVerdictWhat you see
85 to 100SharpText on a card is readable, hair shows strands
60 to 84Slightly softFine for most video calls, small text smears
35 to 59SoftFaces look smoothed, outlines glow
Below 35BlurryFeatures merge, nothing reads at a distance
Above 100Check noiseGrain is adding false edges

For remote work and everyday video conferencing, a score above 60 is enough, because the call app compresses the stream anyway. For content creation, recorded lessons or hosting virtual events, aim for 85 or more.

How to Test Your Webcam Step by Step

Nothing to install: you can test webcam online in your browser, and the webcam test takes under a minute:

  1. Press start and allow camera access when the browser asks.
  2. Pick the right webcam if more than one is connected.
  3. Wait for the webcam viewer to show your live feed and the first score.
  4. Hold a printed page 50 to 70 cm from the camera and keep still for three seconds, so the session peak is set.
  5. Move back to your normal seat and read the score again.
  6. Use Take Photo or fullscreen view to inspect the frame yourself.

Set Lighting, Camera Angle and Eye Level First

The score is only fair if the scene stays the same. Keep the lighting steady, ideally a lamp or window in front of you rather than a bright background behind you. Set the camera angle so the webcam sits at eye level, about an arm's length away, and fix the framing before you start. If your lighting conditions change mid-test, restart it.

Online Webcam Test Results From a Star Chart Example

To show how the numbers behave, we ran this online webcam test on a 24-spoke star chart, a printed pattern of black and white wedges with outlines at every angle. The camera streamed at 1280×720 and the tool scored a 160×160 pixel crop at the chart's centre:

SituationLaplacian varianceScoreVerdict
A. Clean glass, chart sharply focused504.6100.0Sharp (session peak)
B. Chart slightly off the focal plane236.768.5Slightly soft
C. Camera locked on the wall behind91.842.6Soft
D. Fingerprint smear on the glass24.922.2Blurry
E. Same as A, in a dimly lit room1,218.0155.4Check noise

Check row B by hand: \(100 \times \sqrt{236.7 \div 504.6} = 100 \times \sqrt{0.469} = 68.5\). Halving the variance costs about 30 points, and the smear in row D left less than a twentieth of the peak.

Row E is the trap. The chart was as sharp as in row A, but the webcam raised its gain in the dark, and the image noise added thousands of false edges. The Laplacian can't tell grain from detail, so the score jumped past 100. A reading above 100 means "fix the room first", not a sharper camera. Run any webcam test of this kind in steady, bright conditions: a 4K camera in a dark room still loses to a 720p one at a sunny desk.

Recording a Lecture Series: A Real Webcam Test Before Day One

I'm about to record twelve 40-minute statistics lectures with an external 1080p webcam clipped to a monitor 74 cm from my face, and the first draft clip looks soft. The decision is simple: keep this camera, or fix something before recording eight hours of footage. The answer came out as 74.2, slightly soft, fixable without buying anything.

First I set the session peak by holding the printed course outline 58 cm from the camera under my desk lamp. The tool logged a peak Laplacian variance of 731.8. Back in my seat it read 402.6, so the score is \(100 \times \sqrt{402.6 \div 731.8} = 74.2\). I recomputed that by hand and it matched. Since these are recordings, my bar is 85, which means I need a variance of at least \(0.85^2 \times 731.8 = 528.7\) at my seat.

RerunVarianceScore
Seated, automatic mode402.674.2
Seated, focal position locked in the camera app655.394.6
Locked, desk lamp off1,043.9119.4

Locking the focal position cleared the 528.7 threshold comfortably. The lamp-off rerun is the one to watch: 119.4 looks like an improvement, but it is grain, and the clip looks worse.

The less obvious problem is that the score is relative. It compares each frame with the best frame of this session, so it can't tell me the recording app had quietly picked 1280×720. I checked the pixels instead. With a 78-degree camera at 74 cm, the frame is about 1.20 m wide, so my roughly 63 mm eye spacing spans 100.9 pixels at 1920 wide but only 67.3 at 1280. The ISO/IEC 19794-5 face-image standard asks for at least 90 pixels between the eye centres, which the 720p stream misses even at a perfect score.

So my next step is precise: force 1920×1080 in the recorder, keep the focal position locked, leave the lamp on, and rerun before every session. Of all the inputs, resolution matters most here, because a score of 100 on a low-resolution stream only means "as sharp as this stream gets".

What Causes a Blurry Image or Poor Picture Quality

A low score almost always has one of three causes, and each leaves a different pattern in the numbers.

A Dirty Lens or Smudged Cover

Fingerprints and dust spread every outline, so the score stays low wherever you point the camera, as in row D. First, clean the camera lens with a dry microfibre cloth and check that a sliding shutter or screen protector isn't half over it.

Autofocus Hunting and Motion Blur

If the score swings while you sit still, the autofocus is hunting between you and the background, as in row C. Sit closer or turn off auto-framing, which keeps reframing the shot. If the score drops only when you move, that is motion blur from a slow shutter, often with lag and choppy movement. A Logitech or other external webcam usually lets you lock the focal position in its own app.

Low Light, Exposure and Grainy Video

In a dark room the camera lengthens exposure and boosts gain. The feed turns noisy, real outlines soften and the score is fooled upward, as row E showed. Watch for artifacting and flicker from mains-powered lamps too. Low-light grain is how a webcam can auto-adjust its way to blurry video that still looks bright.

Image Quality Readings: Resolution, Frame Rate and Color

Crispness is one part of image quality. A full test also reports these readings, and most of them move the score:

  • Resolution and video standard: the pixel grid, such as 1280×720 (HD). Fewer pixels across your face cap the score's real meaning.
  • Frame rate in fps: under 20 fps usually means longer exposures, so motion smears and the score drops.
  • Quality rating and number of colors: very few colours suggests heavy compression, which wipes out fine outlines.
  • Lightness and luminosity: a dark frame invites the gain noise that inflates the score.
  • Bitrate: caps video quality once a call app compresses the stream, so a high score here can still soften in a call.
  • Built-in microphone: no effect on the score, but moving the webcam back moves its mic too.

Supported Resolutions, Megapixels and Aspect Ratio

A webcam lists several supported resolutions, but a browser or app often picks a low one by default. 1280×720 is 0.92 megapixels, 1920×1080 is 2.07 and 4K is 8.29. Set the highest available resolution before you judge the score, and check that the aspect ratio is 16:9. A webcam resolution tester lists every mode the device supports.

Color Balance, Brightness and Field of View

Poor color balance or high saturation doesn't blur the picture, but it hides texture in skin and hair, lowering image clarity. Check brightness and color depth too. A wide field of view makes your face fill fewer pixels, so a 100-degree webcam looks softer than a 65-degree one at the same resolution.

Check Your Camera Permission, Software and Webcam Settings

If the test shows no picture at all, the problem is access, not the optics. The browser, the operating system and other software can each block the webcam, and the privacy settings on your computer can switch it off entirely.

Allowing Camera Access in Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge

In Chrome and Edge, click the icon left of the address bar and set the camera to Allow. In Safari, allow the camera in the website settings for this page. In Firefox, use the permissions icon in the address bar. On Windows, open Settings > Camera permissions; on Mac, open the Camera list in System Settings; on Linux, make sure your user can open the video device.

Drivers, USB Port and Hardware Faults

If the feed freezes or the score never appears, update the webcam drivers, then try another USB port or cable. Open the Windows Camera app or Photo Booth to see whether the system finds the device. If neither shows a picture on your laptop, try the camera on another computer, or use your smartphone as a webcam to rule out a hardware fault.

Testing Inside Zoom, Teams and Google Meet

Call apps add their own processing software, so finish by checking the app you actually use. Zoom and Google Meet each have a video preview in settings. Turn off background blur and "touch up" filters, which smooth outlines on purpose, and make a short recording. Test your webcam this way after any app update.

Privacy and Browser Support in This Webcam Tester

This webcam tester processes every frame locally in your browser. No video or photo is uploaded, so you can test your webcam on a work machine without sharing anything. It works as a free webcam test in any current browser: Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge. To check your camera setup between readings, a composition grid with rule-of-thirds lines keeps your face inside the scored centre crop, and mirror view or natural view doesn't change the score.

faq.question: Can I run a sharpness and focus test online for free?
faq.answer: Yes. The test runs in your browser with no download or account. Allow camera access when asked and the score updates from your live video.

faq.question: Why is my webcam blurry even though it works?
faq.answer: The usual causes are a smudged lens, autofocus locking on the background, low light that forces long exposures, or an app streaming at a low resolution. Clean the lens first, then check lighting and the resolution your app picked.

faq.question: Why can my focus score go above 100?
faq.answer: The score compares each frame with the sharpest frame in the session. In a dim room the camera raises its gain, and the grain adds false edges, so the variance climbs past the peak. Add light and retest rather than reading it as extra sharpness.

faq.question: Can a webcam pass a basic test but still look soft on calls?
faq.answer: Yes. A camera can show a picture and still struggle with focus, low light or motion. Call apps also compress the stream and may apply smoothing filters, so check the preview in the app you use.

faq.question: Why does my frame rate drop in a dark room?
faq.answer: In low light the camera lengthens each exposure to gather more light, which leaves less time per frame. A 30 fps webcam can fall to 15 fps, and movement then smears.

faq.question: Is my video uploaded during the test?
faq.answer: No. Every frame is analysed locally in your browser and nothing is stored or sent once you close the page.

faq.question: Which browser works best for a webcam focus check?
faq.answer: Current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari all support camera access. If the camera is not detected, check the site permission in the browser and the camera privacy setting in your operating system.

meta_description: Free webcam lighting test in your browser: see if your camera looks too dark or washed out, get a brightness score, and fix your light before calls.
h1: Webcam Lighting Test: Check Exposure and Brightness
subtitle: Click Start Camera on this webcam lighting test to get your Condition label and live Brightness readings.

card.fields_html:
Lighting & Exposure Test

Sit where you normally would for a call and let the reading settle for a couple of seconds

Your camera feed will appear here
Click Start Camera and allow access when your browser asks.

Exposure Reading

Updates a few times a second

—Condition
—Overall Brightness
—Centre Brightness
—Edge Brightness

Cameras auto-adjust exposure continuously, so readings take a second or two to settle after you move or the lighting changes.

What To Do

Advice specific to what the camera is currently seeing

Start the camera to get advice tailored to your current lighting.

content_html:
A room can look bright to your eyes and still leave your face dim on camera, and you won't find out until someone on the other end asks you to turn a lamp on. This lighting and exposure test, a free webcam lighting test, reads your feed for a few seconds and tells you how bright your face actually looks, whether the picture is clipping, and what to move before your next round of video calls or virtual meetings. It takes your real lighting conditions into account, not a guess.

What the Webcam Lighting Test Measures

This webcam check looks at the same video your camera sends to a Zoom call and turns it into numbers you can act on. It runs in your browser, the analysis happens locally on your device, and the video quality reading doesn't depend on your connection. You get one headline score plus a set of supporting readings that explain why the score came out the way it did.

How Average Brightness Becomes a Brightness Score

When you press Start, the page opens your webcam with the browser's getUserMedia API and draws the live feed into a hidden canvas a few times per second. From those sample frames it reads every pixel's red, green and blue values and converts each one to perceived lightness (luma) with the Rec. 709 weights, which favour green because your eyes are most sensitive to it:

$$Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B$$

The average brightness of all pixels is then scaled to a 0-100 range:

$$\text{Score} = \frac{\bar{Y}}{255} \times 100$$

The test reports this brightness score twice: once for the whole picture and once for a face zone in the centre third of the frame, where you normally sit. The second figure matters more, because a bright wall can lift the overall estimated brightness while your face stays in shade. Treat the result as a brightness estimate, not a lab measurement: your webcam's own processing changes the picture before the page ever sees it.

Lightness, Luminosity and Other Camera Readings

Alongside the score, the test lists the readings below. Together they tell you whether a weak result is a light problem or a camera problem.

ReadingWhat it tells you
LightnessHow light the average colour is, from black to white
LuminosityPerceived light level weighted for human vision
Hue and saturationThe colour cast of your light and how strong the colour is
Average RGB colorThe mean red, green and blue values of the image
Number of colorsA low count points to a dark room or poor image quality
Frame rateFrames per second actually delivered; it drops in low light

A grayscale image flattens the colour readings, but the score still works. Sharpness and noise show up as a soft, speckled picture in dim rooms. You can try the image filters to preview how a brightness and contrast change would look, but fixing the light itself always beats boosting it in software, since software gain also boosts noise.

How to Test Your Webcam Before Video Calls

Run the check where you will actually sit, at the time of day you usually take calls. To test webcam lighting properly:

  1. Click Start test and allow camera access when the browser prompt appears.
  2. Pick your camera if you have more than one; the camera preview starts at its native resolution.
  3. Sit in your normal position and look at the webcam for about five seconds while the score settles.
  4. Switch on the mirror preview if you want the view you see in a mirror; others see the unmirrored picture.
  5. Change one thing (a lamp, a blind, your seat), then read the score again.

Close Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet first if they are open, since most systems let only one app hold the camera at a time.

Fixing Camera Access and Permission Errors

A black preview is almost always an access problem, not a light one. Quick troubleshooting:

  • Click the lock or camera icon in the address bar, allow camera use for the site, then reload the page.
  • Quit apps that may still hold the webcam, including OBS and any call app running in the background.
  • Check that camera permission is switched on for your browser in Windows, macOS or Linux privacy settings.
  • Update the webcam driver, or try another USB port and cable for an external camera.
  • Use a current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari; very old browser versions lack the camera API.

Reading Your Lighting and Exposure Test Results

A single webcam test number only helps if you know which band it falls in and why. Read the face-zone score first, then compare it with the score for the whole picture; a large gap between the two is the clearest sign that your setup, not your image quality, is the problem.

Too Dark, Too Bright or Washed Out

The test sorts the face-zone score into five bands:

Face-zone scoreBandWhat you see on camera
0-25Very darkFace in shadow, grainy picture, lost detail
25-40DimUsable, but flat and noisy
40-70BalancedClear skin detail and natural colour
70-85BrightShiny forehead, fading highlights
85-100Blown outWashed out face with white patches

The test also counts clipped pixels. A share above about 2% means the camera is blowing out the highlights somewhere in the picture, while a large share of near-black pixels means it will crush blacks in hair, clothing and shadows. If you see "The room is too dark", add light in front of you; if you see "The image is too bright", dim or move the source pointing at your face.

Why Backlighting and a Bright Window Fool Auto-Brightness

Webcams set their own brightness by metering the whole picture. With a bright window behind you, the camera sees a lot of light and turns its gain down, so the window looks fine and your face goes dark. That is backlighting, and auto-brightness can't solve it because it is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The fix is to change the balance of light, not the camera: face the window instead of sitting with windows behind you, close a blind, or add a light in front that is roughly as strong as the backlight.

Worked Example: An Overexposed Window Behind the Desk

Here is a home desk set against a sunny window. The preview is sampled at 160 × 90, so each reading covers 14,400 pixels.

  • Before: the face zone averages RGB (66, 52, 46). Its luma is 0.2126 × 66 + 0.7152 × 52 + 0.0722 × 46 = 54.5, and 54.5 ÷ 255 × 100 = 21.4, which is very dark. The whole picture still scores 60.6, which looks balanced, because the overexposed window behind scores 83.9 and drags the average up. 9.6% of all pixels (1,382) are clipped.
  • After: the desk is turned 90° so the window sits to the side, and a desk lamp is placed in front. The face zone now averages RGB (176, 138, 118), a luma of 144.6 and a score of 56.7. The whole picture drops to 51.9, the window area to 58.2, and clipped pixels fall to 0.4% (58).

The tonal mix shifted too: dark tones (luma under 64) fell from 31% of pixels to 12%, midtones rose from 52% to 81%, and bright tones dropped from 17% to 7%. The face got 2.6 times brighter while the overall score went down. That is why the test leads with the face zone: judged on the whole picture alone, the before setup would have passed.

Testing Video Conference Lighting Before a Dusk Panel Interview

The interview is at 5:40 pm in late October, on a four-person panel, and the only free room is a converted basement office: one small north-facing window high on the wall and a single ceiling fixture. The question I need answered is simple: is my face bright enough to read, and which lamp position gets it there? The answer turned out to be a desk lamp at 50 cm, which takes the face-zone reading from 28.0 to 52.2.

I run the test at 5:20 pm, sitting exactly where I will sit for the call, with the ceiling light on. The face zone averages RGB (83, 69, 61). Working the luma by hand to check the tool: 0.2126 × 83 + 0.7152 × 69 + 0.0722 × 61 = 71.4, and 71.4 ÷ 255 × 100 = 28.0, which sits in the dim band. The panel would see me, but flat and noisy.

Then I change one input at a time and rerun:

SetupFace RGBFace scoreBand
Ceiling light only83, 69, 6128.0Dim
Desk lamp at 80 cm, in front121, 98, 8640.0Balanced (edge)
Same lamp moved to 50 cm158, 128, 11152.2Balanced

What stands out is the last step. Moving the lamp from 80 cm to 50 cm multiplies the light on my face by (80 ÷ 50)² = 2.56, yet the score rises only 1.3 times. Two things eat the difference. Camera values are gamma-encoded, so 2.56 times the light raises the pixel value by about 2.561/2.2 = 1.53, which would put the score near 61.3 with the camera's settings frozen. The rest is the webcam's own auto-adjustment turning its gain down once more light arrives. So a score that barely moves after you add a lamp doesn't mean the lamp failed; the camera is quietly cancelling part of it, and you only see the full gain when exposure is locked in the camera app.

My judgement call: I stop at 52.2 rather than pushing the lamp closer. Broadcast camera operators commonly set zebra warnings at 70% for skin highlights, and at 61 or above my forehead would start getting close to that in this setup. The number I actually watch is the gap to 40, the bottom of the balanced band, because daylight from that window will be gone by 5:40 and the face reading falls without it. I rerun at 5:35 to confirm the lamp alone still holds the face inside the balanced band.

How to Improve Your Webcam Light

Better webcam light comes mostly from where your lights sit, not how many you own. The same rules hold for good video conference lighting at any budget: light from the front, soft rather than hard, and dimmer behind you than in front.

Put Your Front Light Source at Eye Level

Place your main light source in front of you, slightly above eye level and just behind the screen, so it lights your face evenly. A window gives natural light by day; a desk lamp works after dark. Raise the laptop or monitor so the lens sits at eye level too, which stops the camera looking up at you from below. If you can only add one thing, add a front light: it raises the face score more than any camera setting can.

Ring Light, Soft Light and a Diffuser

A ring light wraps light evenly around the lens and is the simplest desk upgrade. Pick one with adjustable light intensity, and set it slightly to the side if it reflects in your glasses. For soft light, use a bigger source or bounce it off a wall. Harsh light from a bare bulb shows up in the test as a high clipped-pixel share; a clip-on diffuser or an LED panel with a frosted cover will diffuse the beam, smooth skin tone and bring that share back down on a rerun.

From 2-Point Lighting to 3-Point Lighting

In a two-light setup, the key light is your brightest source at about 45° to one side, and the fill light sits opposite at roughly half its strength to soften the shadows the key creates. A third light, a back light or rim light behind you, lifts you off the background: the classic studio look scaled down for a home office. Rerun the test after adding each light; the face-zone score should stay between 40 and 70 with clipping under 2%.

Avoid Overhead Lighting and Busy Backgrounds

Ceiling fixtures and fluorescent lights throw shadows under your eyes and nose, so harsh overhead light alone rarely scores well in the face zone even when the room seems bright. Keep the background a little darker than your face, and clear clutter from behind you. Wear neutral colors: bright white shirts push the camera to darken everything, and black ones do the opposite. A colored wall bounces a matching tint onto your skin. Use the rule-of-thirds or composition grid view to place your eyes about a third of the way down the frame. If the picture looks hazy, clean the camera lens.

How Webcam Hardware Handles Poor Lighting Conditions

Hardware sets the limit on how well a camera copes when light is scarce. A typical laptop webcam or built-in camera has a tiny sensor and gets grainy fast; an external webcam on an external monitor usually does better, and a recent smartphone used as a webcam often beats both.

Sensor Size and Lowlight Performance

The biggest factor in lowlight performance is how much light the camera collects. A larger sensor gathers more light per pixel than a small one with the same megapixels, a wider aperture such as f/1.9 lets in more than f/2.0, and a glass lens resolves cleaner detail. Two cameras can return the same face-zone score in one room while the small laptop camera looks far rougher, so a speckled picture at a balanced score points to a hardware limit, not a light problem. Heavy image processing can hurt color accuracy; bokeh and autofocus don't change the reading, and a wide field of view can pull a window into the shot.

Low-Light Correction, Resolution and Color Temperature

Most webcams include low-light correction, which raises gain in dim rooms. It brightens the picture at the cost of noise and a lower frame rate: a camera rated at 30 fps may drop to 15 in a dark room, which makes video look choppy. A higher resolution won't fix poor light or image quality either; 4K is worth having for reframing, but most call apps send 1080p or 720p, and a well-lit 1080p picture looks better than a dim 4K one. Match the color temperature of your lamps to your daylight (around 5000-5600 K) so your face isn't half blue and half orange.

Online Webcam Test Privacy and When to Run It

Your privacy stays intact: the online webcam test processes every frame locally, so no video is uploaded, stored or shared, and stopping the test releases the webcam. Run the webcam lighting test whenever the setup changes:

  • Before job interviews, client meetings or a webinar you are presenting.
  • Before streaming video or going on a live stream.
  • After moving desks or rooms, or adding a new lamp.
  • At a different time of day, since window light changes by the hour.

Every webcam and browser handles video slightly differently, so treat the score as a guide for comparing setups, not an absolute value.

faq.question: How accurate is the brightness score?
faq.answer: It is an estimate from your camera's preview, not a light-meter reading. Your webcam's own auto-adjustment changes the picture before the test sees it, so use the score to compare setups in the same room rather than as an absolute value.

faq.question: Why do I look dark with a bright window behind me?
faq.answer: The camera sets its brightness for the whole picture. A bright window behind you makes it turn its gain down, which leaves your face in shade. Turn to face the window, close a blind, or add a light in front of you.

faq.question: What brightness reading counts as good lighting?
faq.answer: On the 0-255 scale, 80 to 180 is good lighting. Below 50 is too dark, 50 to 80 is dim, 180 to 220 is bright with fading colors, and above 220 is overexposed.

faq.question: What do clipped highlights and crushed blacks mean?
faq.answer: Clipped highlights are pixels so bright they turn pure white and lose detail; crushed blacks are pixels so dark they turn pure black. A few percent of each is normal, but large shares mean the light is too strong or too weak in part of the picture.

faq.question: Why does my frame rate drop in a dark room?
faq.answer: In low light the camera keeps each frame open longer to gather more light, so fewer frames fit into each second. A 30 fps webcam can fall to 15 fps or lower, which makes video look choppy. More light usually brings the frame rate back.

faq.question: What lighting is best for video calls?
faq.answer: A soft light in front of you at about eye level, such as a lamp or ring light, usually looks best. Avoid harsh overhead light and strong backlight from windows behind you.

faq.question: Is my video uploaded during the test?
faq.answer: No. The preview is processed locally in your browser, nothing is uploaded or stored, and stopping the test releases the camera.

meta_description: Is my camera on? This free online webcam test shows whether your webcam is live, held by another app or blocked, and which permissions your browser granted.
h1: Is My Camera On? Webcam In-Use Privacy Check & Webcam Test
subtitle: Click Run Check to answer is my camera on — instantly see if it's free, in use, or blocked.

card.fields_html:
Camera In-Use Privacy Check

Tests whether your camera is free to use right now, or already held by another app

Click Run Check. This briefly requests camera access and releases it immediately — nothing is recorded or previewed.

What This Actually Tests

Browsers don't let any website see which app is using your camera — only whether a new request to use it succeeds or fails. This check can't detect spyware or confirm anything is secretly recording you. What it can tell you: if the request fails with "already in use," some other running application currently has an exclusive lock on the camera — that's usually a video-call app left open in the background, not something malicious.

If you're worried about unauthorised access, the indicator light next to your camera is the most reliable signal — see the guide alongside this.

Indicator Light & Privacy Panel Guide

WindowsGreen LED lights whenever any app uses the camera. Check Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera for which apps have permission.
macOSGreen LED next to the camera lights whenever it's active. Check System Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera.
AndroidA green dot appears in the status bar when the camera or mic is active. Check Settings → Privacy → Permission manager → Camera.
iOSA green (camera) or orange (mic) dot appears at the top of the screen. Check Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera.

content_html:
Is my camera on right now? If you suspect your webcam is quietly switched on, the Camera In-Use Privacy Check lets you check if your camera is live, held by another program or blocked, and shows which permissions your browser has actually granted, with no sign-up. If the camera is working, you also see its resolution, FPS and lighting; if it isn't, close whatever is holding it (a forgotten call or a screen recorder) and refresh. It is a quick online check worth running before video calls.

How the Camera In-Use Privacy Check Works

When you press Start, the tool asks your browser for its list of media devices. That list tells it how many webcams exist before any is switched on, and the device selector (a dropdown menu above the webcam viewer) lets you pick one when there are several, which is common on a laptop with a docked USB webcam or a smartphone with front and rear lenses.

Next it requests a video stream from the selected webcam. One of three things happens:

  • A video track arrives and plays in real time, so the webcam is free and now on for this page only.
  • The browser refuses with NotAllowedError, so access is blocked by you, the browser or the system.
  • The request fails with NotReadableError, the classic sign the webcam is held by another program.

Pressing Test my cam again re-runs the whole check. It works in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge with no software to install.

Allow Access When the Browser Asks

The first time you run it, a pop-up or prompt appears near the address bar. Choose Allow to allow access for this site; the camera permission is then remembered until you revoke it. If you clicked Block by mistake, fix the setting described below and reload the page so the request runs again.

Reading Your Webcam Test Results

Once live, the camera feed appears in the preview window and the webcam test fills in a status table. Here is what each row means:

CheckExample readingWhat it tells you
Camera permission stategranted / prompt / deniedWhether this site may open the webcam
Cameras found3 (built-in, USB, virtual)Every webcam the browser can see
In use by another appYes or NoWhether the webcam is already streaming elsewhere
Resolution and megapixels1920 × 1080, 2.07 MPDetail the webcam actually delivers
Aspect ratio16:9Frame shape sent to your call
Frame rate29.4 fpsSmoothness of the stream
BrightnessAverage pixel levelWhether your lighting is too dark
Built-in microphoneDetected / noneWhether the webcam carries its own microphone

The numbers come from two simple calculations on the live frames:

$$\text{Megapixels} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height}}{1{,}000{,}000} \qquad \text{FPS} = \frac{\text{frames counted}}{\text{seconds}}$$

In our example, a USB webcam streaming \(1920 \times 1080\) gives 2.07 MP, and 147 frames counted over 5 seconds gives 29.4 fps, close enough to 30 that video quality and image quality both look fine. If the webcam is working but the picture is dark, take a couple of snapshots under different lamps before you blame the hardware.

When the Camera Is Used by Another App

Most webcams accept one client at a time, so if Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet, Skype or the built-in camera app is open, the check reports the webcam as being used by another application. A third-party application such as a virtual-background tool can also hold it silently in the background. Close other video apps, including tray icons and browser tabs from an earlier call, then run the check again. If it still shows busy, restarting the computer releases it.

Is the Webcam LED a Reliable Privacy Signal?

On most laptops the LED is wired to the webcam's power and lights whenever the sensor runs. Treat it as a hint, not proof: some external models let software switch their LED lights off, and a closed shutter shows a black image while the webcam streams. A muted or black preview with the light on means it is on but covered. Comparing the LED, the browser's camera icon and this check gives you three independent signals. (Mirror view only flips the picture on your side and changes nothing about who can see you.)

Check If Your Camera Is Watching: Tracing a Late-Night Webcam Light

It is 8:42 pm, every window on my Windows 11 laptop is closed, and the white light beside the built-in webcam is on. The question is simple: is something watching, and which program is it? The short answer from the camera in-use check: the built-in camera was held by a background virtual-background utility, not by a website, and closing it released the camera within seconds.

Here is the sequence I follow:

  1. Run the check with the built-in camera selected. Browser permission reads granted, but the stream request fails with NotReadableError, so the camera is busy, not blocked.
  2. Cross-check outside the browser: Settings, Privacy & security, Camera, Recent activity. One desktop app is listed as currently in use, started at 8:37 pm. No browser appears there, which rules out a forgotten tab.
  3. Quit the utility from the system tray, then rerun. The LED goes off, then on again only when the check asks for the stream.

The rerun reports 1280 × 720, which is 921,600 pixels or 0.92 MP, and 211 frames in 7.5 seconds, 28.1 fps. That meets the 720p HD standard, so this webcam is fine for calls once nothing else owns it.

I then switch to a USB webcam on the same desk, and the numbers surprise me:

RunResolutionFrames / secondsFrame rate
USB, desk lamp off2560 × 1440 (3.69 MP)89 / 614.8 fps
USB, desk lamp on2560 × 1440 (3.69 MP)179 / 629.8 fps

Same camera, same resolution, half the frame rate. In dim light auto-exposure lengthens each frame, so a low reading here is a lighting problem, not a fault or a sign of a second app. That is the edge case worth knowing: a low frame rate alone never proves another program is sharing the camera; only NotReadableError plus a matching entry in the system's activity list does.

My judgement after this run: the LED told me something was on, but only the error code and the Windows activity log together told me what. If Recent activity had shown nothing while the error persisted, I would suspect the driver instead and reinstall it before blaming any software.

Browser Permissions and the Camera Icon in Chrome, Firefox and Safari

Every browser keeps its own list of webcam permissions per site, so a webcam can work in one browser and fail in another.

  • Chrome and Edge: click the lock button (or tune icon) at the left of the URL bar, then set Camera to Allow. For all sites, open chrome://settings/content/camera.
  • Firefox: the camera icon sits to the left of the address; click it to clear a blocked entry. Defaults live under about:preferences#privacy.
  • Safari: open Settings, then Websites, then Camera, and choose Allow or Ask for this site.

If a site shows camera access denied even though you never clicked Block, the browser itself may lack permission from the system. Blocked camera access at that level hides the prompt entirely, which is why the next section matters.

Check Camera and Microphone Permissions Together

Browsers usually ask for the camera and the microphone in one prompt, and you can grant one while refusing the other. When you check camera permissions, glance at the microphone entry too: a call app with a working picture and a silent mic usually has the camera allowed and the microphone blocked. This check lists both states, so a split decision is easy to spot.

Camera Access in Operating System Privacy Settings

Above the browser sits the operating system, which can switch the webcam off for every program at once. These privacy settings override anything you allow in the browser, so a webcam disabled in system settings looks the same as a missing one. Desktop apps and browsers each need their own switch turned on.

Windows 11 and 10: Let Apps Access Your Camera

In Windows 11, open Start, then Settings, then Privacy & security, then Camera. Turn on Camera access and Let apps access your camera, then make sure your browser is listed. In Windows 10, the page is Settings, Privacy, Camera; set Camera access for this device to On and allow desktop apps further down the page.

macOS Security & Privacy and Linux

On macOS, open System Settings (System Preferences on older versions), then Privacy & Security (the Security & Privacy pane, Privacy tab, on Mojave to Monterey), choose Camera and tick your browser. On Linux, check that your user can read /dev/video0 and that no other process has it open.

Webcam Not Working? Troubleshooting an External Webcam

When the check finds no camera at all, work through the likely causes from the cheapest fix to the most expensive. These steps cover a built-in or external webcam alike:

  1. Check your webcam is selected in the device selector, and that any physical on/off switch or shutter is open.
  2. Connection problem: reseat the web camera in a different USB port, and try another USB cable if it detaches.
  3. Driver issues: open Device Manager, look for the webcam under Cameras or Imaging devices, and update or reinstall its drivers.
  4. Disabled device: if it shows as disabled in Device Manager, enable it and start the check again.
  5. Software conflicts: if the check still fails after you update the browser and operating system, troubleshoot in a private window with extensions off.
  6. Hardware failure: if a second computer can't see the web camera either, the webcam itself has failed.

Privacy and Security: What a Free Cam Check Never Stores

A privacy check that uploaded your camera feed would defeat its own purpose. This online webcam test runs locally: frames are analysed in your browser and kept only in device memory, nothing is uploaded or stored on a server, and closing the tab discards every reading. It makes no recordings and uses no account, so this free webcam test needs no data from you. You can record or save a snapshot only if you choose to, and the file stays on your machine. It reads frames only while this tab is open, the security bar any webcam test tool or webcam testing tool should meet: private by design, secure by default.

Test Your Webcam Before Video Calls

Run it a minute before any video conferencing session or before you record a tutorial, to test your camera: the right webcam is selected, nothing else holds it, and your lighting works. A quick test my webcam habit also pays off after installing a new app, since that is when an unexpected program most often grabs the webcam.

faq.question: How do I check if my camera is on?
faq.answer: Start the test and allow camera access when your browser asks. If a live picture appears, the camera is free and on for this page only. If the test reports the camera as busy, another app is already using it.

faq.question: Why does my webcam say it is being used by another application?
faq.answer: Most cameras serve one app at a time. Close Zoom, Teams, Skype, the camera app or any virtual-camera tool, including ones sitting in the system tray, then reload the page. Restarting your computer frees a camera that stays stuck.

faq.question: How do I change camera permissions in Chrome?
faq.answer: Click the lock or tune icon at the left of the URL bar and set Camera to Allow. To change the default for every site, open chrome://settings/content/camera.

faq.question: How do I allow the camera in Firefox or Safari?
faq.answer: In Firefox, click the camera icon beside the address and clear the blocked entry, or use about:preferences#privacy. In Safari, open Settings, then Websites, then Camera, and choose Allow or Ask for the site.

faq.question: How do I give desktop apps and browsers camera access on Windows or Mac?
faq.answer: On Windows 11, open Settings, Privacy & security, Camera and turn on Camera access and Let apps access your camera. On a Mac, open System Settings, Privacy & Security, Camera and tick your browser or app.

faq.question: Can I check an external webcam?
faq.answer: Yes. Plug it in, then pick it from the camera list before you start the test. If it does not appear, try another USB port or cable and check its driver in Device Manager.

faq.question: Is my video uploaded or stored?
faq.answer: No. Everything runs in your browser and stays in your device's memory. Nothing is uploaded or saved, and closing the tab discards every reading.

meta_description: Check used phone camera quality online before you pay. Test front and rear cameras for dead pixels, haze, dust and autofocus faults, free in your browser.
h1: Check Used Phone Camera: Inspection Test Before You Buy
subtitle: Click Start Camera to check used phone camera quality through a guided 7-step checklist, marking each Pass or Fail as you go.

card.fields_html:
Step 1 of 7 — Select the Lens

Choose which camera you want to inspect

Your camera feed will appear here

Start the camera, then use the dropdown to pick the lens you want to inspect. Repeat this whole checklist once per lens if the phone has more than one (wide, ultra-wide, telephoto, front).

Click Start Camera and allow access when your browser asks.

Checklist

Click any step to jump to it

Summary

Updates as you complete steps

0Passed
0Failed
7Pending

Useful to show a seller, or to keep for your own records before buying. Nothing here is uploaded — everything stays on this page.

content_html:
A seller can make a screen look new, but the camera is harder to fake. This used phone camera inspection streams a live image from every camera in your browser, so as the buyer you can spot defects like bad pixels, haze and blurry shots before you pay. Six minutes of checks is enough to check used phone camera condition and see how much to knock off the offer.

How the Used Phone Camera Inspection Works

Open the page on the phone you're buying, tap start and allow camera access when the browser asks. Keep the phone's own camera app closed so the camera test gets the hardware to itself. A full pass takes about six minutes:

  • 0:00 – open the page and allow access
  • 0:40 – main rear lens on a bright, detailed scene
  • 1:50 – sweep through every rear unit
  • 3:10 – front camera, close and at arm's length
  • 4:00 – one shot in a dim room
  • 5:00 – a 10-second video clip, then review

Check the Rear Camera, Then the Front

Start with the main rear camera, since it does most of the work. Switch through the rear lenses one by one: the main unit, the ultra-wide and, on higher-end models, the telephoto. Then flip to the selfie camera.

Capture Test Images and Zoom In

The preview hides small flaws, so take a few photos and open them magnified to 100%, checking corners and plain areas. Scanning a barcode from 10 cm is a quick close-range check, and saved shots land in the camera roll like screenshots for a later look on a bigger screen.

Run It Privately on Android or iOS

The feed stays on the phone, on Android and iOS alike. Close any app using the camera in the background first, or the page may not get access.

Common Camera Module Defects to Look For

Some faults mean the camera module is failing; others are cheap fixes or simply dirt. Knowing which is which keeps you from walking away from a good phone or overpaying for damaged camera hardware.

Malfunction: A Black Screen or Corrupted Image Buffer

The clearest malfunction is a camera that won't start or shows only black. A rarer sign is a picture full of stripes or fragments of another image, meaning the image buffer is being fed garbage. Either way it's a failed part, not a setting.

Hot or Dead Pixels on the Image Sensor

Aim at a plain, evenly lit surface and look for dots that stay put when you move the phone. Bright dots are hot; dark ones are dead. A couple are tolerable, but a cluster near the centre of the sensor shows up in every shot.

Spots or Haze from Dust and Cover Glass Scratches

Soft round blotches fixed in place usually mean dust inside the module. A milky haze over the whole picture points to the cover glass instead: fine scratches or grime on the outer window. Wipe the lens and retest. These artifacts often appear or vanish as you change zoom, because the phone hands off to a different physical camera.

Out-of-Focus Shots and a Stuck Autofocus

Tap to focus on something near, then across the room. If close objects are sharp but distant ones stay soft, or the reverse, the focusing mechanism is likely jammed. A faulty autofocus can still look fine at one distance, so an out-of-focus result at only one range still counts.

Slow Frame Updates and Missing Cameras

A choppy preview often means another app is holding the camera or the phone is overheating. If a rear unit never appears, recheck in the built-in app before calling it a fault; some pages only see some cameras.

A Camera Test That Caught a Faulty Telephoto on a Marketplace Phone

The decision on the table: pay $338 for a two-year-old phone with a 3x telephoto, bought mainly for concert shots from the back of a hall. The answer, ten minutes later, is an offer of $273.10, because the telephoto only focuses at close range.

I meet the seller at a café by the window, open the camera test on their phone and allow access. The main rear camera streams 1920×1080 at a steady 29.7 fps against a nominal 30, and the ultra-wide and front camera are clean. Then I tap 3x and frame a menu board about 1.2 m away. Sharp. On paper, a pass.

Here's the trap I watch for. A phone hands short-range zoom shots to the main camera with a digital crop, because the telephoto can't focus that close. So a 3x test at arm's length may never touch the telephoto at all. I step outside and aim at a street sign roughly 9 m away instead. Now the image stays soft whatever I tap, and covering the telephoto window with a finger blacks out the preview, which confirms that module is the one streaming.

Target distanceUnit doing the workResult
1.2 m, 3xMain camera, croppedSharp
9 m, 3xTelephotoSoft at every tap

That's the stuck-focus pattern from the defects list: fine at one distance, useless at the distance I bought it for. A local repair shop quotes $64.90 for the telephoto module over the phone. That is 19.2% of the ask. My own rule is to walk away if a single repair passes 25% of the price, which here is $84.50, so the phone stays on the table at $338 − $64.90 = $273.10.

The judgement call: for most buyers a soft telephoto is a discount, not a deal breaker. For me it's the main reason to buy, so if the seller refuses the repair-adjusted price, I pass. And one caveat: in dim light many phones switch away from the telephoto too, so run that distance check in daylight or the result proves nothing.

Manual vs Automated Smartphone Camera Checks

A dead camera is obvious. Haze and soft detail are not, and two people can disagree about the same photo. That's the gap automated testing closes for resellers.

Why Manual Testing Needs Repeatable Conditions

Manual testing works best with a fixed scene: the same ambient lighting, distance and target for every phone, such as a uniform white sheet for spots and small print for detail. Compare the captured images side by side. A repeatable setup turns "looks a bit soft" into a fair call.

How Functional Testing Scores Sharpness

Refurbishing labs use functional testing rigs that photograph fixed targets under controlled light. A high-contrast chart gives a sharpness reading and a plain lit target a uniformity reading, so numerical analysis rates every unit the same way. Borrow the idea: shoot the same print and sheet on this phone and on one you trust.

Where Diagnostics Fit When You Buy a Pre-Owned Smartphone

Professional diagnostics check far more than the camera, but the camera is often where pre-owned smartphones hide their worst damage.

Private Sales and Marketplace Listings

On a marketplace listing, you're the one checking. Meet in daylight, run the test on the spot, and don't rely on the listing's photos. If photography is why you're buying a second-hand flagship, give the camera the most time.

Refurbishers, Buyback and Trade-In Programs

Refurbishers, carrier trade-in desks and buyback programs process used devices at scale. Their certified units have passed a standard check, and refurbished stock usually carries a warranty, but a two-minute camera check on arrival is still worth it.

Reading a Device History Report

Many resellers include a device history report. Start with the repair history: a replaced camera part tells you which unit to test hardest, and a non-original one on a device sold as untouched is a reason to ask questions. Then glance at the IMEI, carrier blacklist and battery lines.

Turning Camera Condition into a Fair Price

Say a three-year-old flagship is listed at an asking price of $412. The check finds faint haze on the ultra-wide only, from debris inside that unit, plus one hairline scratch on the camera cover. A repair shop quotes $88 for the module and $27 for the glass, so a fair offer is $412 − $88 − $27 = $297.

Grading Second-Hand Smartphone Cameras

Resellers fold the camera into an overall grade. A flawless camera keeps the top grade despite light body wear; a camera fault drops the phone a grade or more, whatever the cosmetic grade says. Rate the cameras on their own and use that grade, not the seller's description, to set your number.

faq.question: How do I check the camera on a used phone before buying it?
faq.answer: Open the camera test in the phone's own browser, allow camera access and watch the live feed. Switch between the front and rear cameras, take a snapshot and record a short clip, then enter what you saw here to get a pass or fail for each check.

faq.question: Is a browser camera test enough to inspect a used phone?
faq.answer: It's a strong first check: it confirms each camera is detected, streams at its expected resolution and captures a clean picture. For a deeper look, also shoot in dim light, zoom in on snapshots to look for dust, haze or scratches, and test focus at near and far distances.

faq.question: Why does the rear or front camera not show up?
faq.answer: Usually the browser was denied camera permission, another app is holding the camera, or the phone only exposes some of its cameras to web pages. Check the Cameras Found count, close other camera apps and reload. If a camera is still missing, recheck it in the phone's built-in camera app.

faq.question: What does the Resolution ≥ 720p check mean?
faq.answer: It passes when the live stream is at least 1280×720. A lower figure can mean a weak sensor, a damaged camera or the browser falling back to a reduced stream, so retest in good light before treating it as a fault.

faq.question: Why is the frame rate low?
faq.answer: Frame rate is frames counted divided by the seconds counted. A low rate often means another app is using the camera in the background, the phone is throttling, or the room is too dark, since each frame then needs a longer exposure.

faq.question: Why does the torch show N/A?
faq.answer: Torch control through the browser only works on some Android phones; iOS Safari doesn't expose it to web pages. N/A here doesn't mean the flash is broken, so test it in the phone's camera app instead.

faq.question: Are my photos or videos uploaded anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The camera test runs locally in your browser. Snapshots and recordings stay on the phone, and closing the tab clears them.
