meta_description: Run a free phone flashlight test in your browser. Switch your rear LED on and off, confirm the flash fires and see why the torch button is grayed out.
h1: Phone Flashlight Test: Check Your Flash and Torch Online
subtitle: Click Turn Torch On on this phone flashlight test to check your rear LED flash instantly.

card.fields_html:
Flash & Torch Test

Starts your rear camera, since torch is only ever exposed on a rear-facing lens

Your camera feed will appear here
Click Start Camera and allow access when your browser asks.

Full-Screen White Light

A screen-brightness alternative when torch control isn't available

Most phones don't let a website control the physical LED flash directly — iOS Safari never exposes it at all, and only some Android browsers do. This turns your whole screen into a bright white light instead, useful as a close-range light source or a substitute for the torch this page can't reach.

Testing the Real Flash

When browser torch control isn't supported

To test the actual LED flash hardware (not just this page's ability to control it), open your phone's native Camera app, switch to video or flashlight mode, and toggle the flash there. If it doesn't light up from the native app either, that points to an actual hardware fault rather than a browser limitation.

content_html:
A flash and torch test tells you in seconds whether your phone's rear LED torch still works. To run this phone flashlight test, tap the button above, accept the browser's camera prompt and switch the LED on and off: if the flash fires and stays bright, the torch is accessible and the hardware on this device is fine.

How to Run the Flash and Torch Test and Confirm the Flash Fires

The torch test needs no app:

  • Press the power on/off button with the lens pointed away from your eyes.
  • Watch the back of the phone, not the live preview. A flashlight test only passes when the LED itself lights.
  • Toggle it three times; a light that works only once is faulty too.

Camera Access, Permissions and Site Settings

Browsers control the flash through the camera, so the page asks for camera access first. Accept the permission prompt, or tap the camera icon in the address bar if you dismissed it. If you blocked it earlier, reset the camera permission:

  • Chrome desktop on Windows: Privacy & Security, then Site settings, then set Camera to Allow.
  • Android: Settings, Apps, your browser, Permissions, then Allow while using app.

Phone Flashlight Torch Control on Android Chrome and iOS Safari

No web page can flip the LED directly. The test opens the camera with getUserMedia, reads its capabilities with getCapabilities and looks for a torch property. If that capability exists, it calls applyConstraints with torch set to true. These standard web APIs come from the MediaStreamTrack spec, so support depends on the browser, not on how healthy your phone flashlight is:

BrowserRear lens torchFront lens torch
Chrome on an Android smartphoneYes, when reportedRarely
Safari on iPhone (iOS)Generally not exposedNo
Desktop browsersNo flashNo

Rear Camera vs Front Camera for the Torch

The flash LED sits beside the main lens, so test with the back camera. Front cameras almost never report a torch; a selfie "flash" is just display backlighting. On phones with several rear cameras, the browser may open a wide or zoom lens with no torch attached, so switch lenses first.

Reading Your Flashlight Test Result

If the LED stays dark, the error usually names the cause.

Torch Button Grayed Out or Disabled

A grayed out button means the browser never reported a torch, which is expected on iPhone, on the selfie lens and on laptops. The browser disabled it, not a broken LED, so retry in Chrome on Android with the rear lens.

Camera in Use or Not Readable Errors

This error means another app holds exclusive access to the camera. Close video calls, camera apps and any other browser tab using the lens, then reload.

Checking a Used Phone's Flash LED Before Paying

I'm standing in a café with a second-hand Android phone listed at $186, and the only question is whether to hand over the cash. The seller says the flash "works fine." The flashlight test on this page lets me check that in two minutes, without installing anything on someone else's phone.

I open the page in Chrome, accept the camera prompt and pick the rear lens. The torch button is active, so the browser can control the LED. Three manual toggles: on, on, then dark on the third press. One miss in three is not enough to walk away on, so I switch to SOS mode, because it toggles the LED far faster than my thumb can.

That turns a three-press check into a stress test of the torch: at a 0.2-second dot, SOS mode switches the LED on 153 times in two minutes, against my 3 manual presses. A slower dot gives fewer chances to catch a fault:

Dot lengthSOS cycleLED switch-ons in 2 minutes
0.2 s6.8 s153
0.3 s10.2 s99

The LED drops 4 flashes, all in the second minute, while the phone is in my hand and the cable end of the case flexes slightly. That pattern reads like a loose connection rather than a burnt-out LED, and it is exactly the camera-module fault a bench test would confirm. I budget $64.90 for a replacement rear camera module, so I offer $121.10 and we settle at $122.

One caveat before trusting a dark LED at all: many phones block the flash when the battery is low or the body is hot. If the battery reads under 15%, a failed run means nothing. Charge to at least 20% and rerun the same LED check before you count any miss against the phone; here the battery showed 68%, so the 4 misses stand.

What a Dead LED Torch Means for Repair

If the button is active, permission is granted and the LED stays dark, software is ruled out. A dead flash LED usually points to a camera-module fault or a damaged connector, since on many phones the LED shares a board or flex cable with the camera. This is a self-check, not a full diagnosis: board-level faults need a bench test with proper diagnostics before any repair. Run two flashlight tests a few minutes apart; an LED flash light that works once and fails the next time is an intermittent fault worth reporting. A faint glow is a fail too; this flashlight / torch test covers hardware only.

Camera Flash Light Modes: Steady, Strobe and SOS

Once the LED passes, steady mode holds full brightness, strobe pulses it at a set strobe frequency, and the emergency SOS or beacon mode flashes three short, three long, three short. With a 0.2-second dot, a dash lasts 0.6 seconds and one SOS takes 5.4 seconds before a 1.4-second pause. Keep strobe slow around people with photosensitive epilepsy and use the auto-off timer.

White Screen Light When There Is No LED

With no usable torch, switch the light source to a white screen light: one bright screen color at full brightness. Far dimmer than a flash light, it still works on laptops and iPhones where torch control is blocked.

Privacy When You Test the Flashlight

This camera and flashlight test runs locally in your browser with no uploads. The video stays on your device, nothing is recorded, and the camera closes when you leave, so you can test the flashlight as often as you like without a privacy trade-off.

Resolution and Frame Rate in a Camera Test

The page also reads the stream with getSettings, which confirms the browser opened the rear-facing lens. The resolution and frame rate shown are what the camera driver negotiated with the browser, often below the sensor's physical maximum, so a lower number isn't a fault.

faq.question: Can I test my phone's flashlight from a browser?
faq.answer: Yes, on Android. Chrome exposes torch control through the camera's MediaStreamTrack capabilities, so the page can switch the rear LED on and off once you allow camera access. iPhone browsers generally don't expose the torch.

faq.question: Why is the torch button grayed out?
faq.answer: Your browser or the selected camera didn't report a torch. That's expected on iPhone, on front cameras and on most desktop browsers. Switch to the rear camera in Chrome on Android and try again.

faq.question: Does the flash and torch test record anything?
faq.answer: No. The camera stream is used only to control the LED and stays on your device. Nothing is recorded or uploaded.

faq.question: What does it mean if the LED never lights?
faq.answer: If the torch button is active and camera access is granted but the LED stays dark, the flash LED or camera module is likely faulty. A browser check is a quick self-check, so have a repair shop bench-test it.

faq.question: Why does it say the camera is in use?
faq.answer: Another app or browser tab already has the camera. Close video calls, camera apps and other tabs using the camera, then reload the page.

faq.question: How long is one SOS flash cycle?
faq.answer: In SOS mode each dot lasts 333 ms and each dash three times that. One S-O-S takes 27 units plus a 7-unit pause, about 11.3 seconds before it repeats.

faq.question: What can I use if my phone has no flash?
faq.answer: Switch the light source to Screen Light. It fills the display with a bright colour you choose, which works on laptops and iPhones where the LED torch can't be controlled.

meta_description: Webcam resolution chart from QVGA to 8K: width and height in pixels, megapixels and aspect ratio for each standard, plus what 720p, 1080p and 4K need.
h1: Webcam Resolution Chart: Standards from QVGA to 8K
subtitle: Click Highlight My Camera's Maximum on this webcam resolution chart to see where your camera lands among every Dimensions and Megapixels standard.

card.fields_html:
Webcam Resolution Standards

Every common video resolution from QQVGA to 8K, sortable and searchable — click a column heading to sort

content_html:
Spec sheets throw around names like WXGA, nHD and DCI 4K as if everyone knows what they mean. This webcam resolution standards reference lines up every common format your webcam might report, with its exact pixel dimensions, shape and megapixel count, so this webcam resolution chart shows at a glance what each resolution actually delivers.

Webcam Resolution Standards Reference Chart

The chart below lists the formats you will meet in webcam settings, video apps and test tools, ordered from smallest to largest pixel count. Most of these names started life as computer display modes or broadcast formats and were later borrowed for webcams and digital cameras, which is why the naming feels inconsistent.

StandardWidth × height (px)Aspect ratioMegapixelsWhere you see it
QCIF176 × 14411:90.03Early video phones
Video CD (NTSC)352 × 24022:150.08Legacy video files
QVGA320 × 2404:30.08Thumbnails, very low bandwidth
nHD / 360p640 × 36016:90.23Small call tiles
VGA640 × 4804:30.31Older built-in cameras
DVD NTSC720 × 4803:20.35Standard-definition video
SVGA800 × 6004:30.48Basic USB webcams
XGA1024 × 7684:30.79Document capture modes
HD / 720p1280 × 72016:90.92Entry-level laptop cameras
WXGA1280 × 8008:51.02Some notebook sensors
SXGA1280 × 10245:41.31Still-photo modes
Square 10801080 × 10801:11.17Square social clips
UXGA1600 × 12004:31.922 MP still images
FHD / 1080p1920 × 108016:92.07Mainstream external webcams
QHD / 1440p2560 × 144016:93.69Mid-range streaming cameras
UHD / 4K3840 × 216016:98.29Premium webcams
DCI 4K4096 × 2160256:135 (about 1.9:1)8.85Cinema capture
5K5120 × 288016:914.75High-end monitors
8K UHD7680 × 432016:933.18Broadcast and image resolutions for large screens

Two patterns stand out. Older 4:3 standards such as SVGA, XGA and UXGA come from monitors; modern webcam modes are mostly 16:9. And the jump between rungs is not linear: 4K holds four times the pixels of 1080p, not twice.

How Width and Height Become Megapixels and Aspect Ratio

Every entry in the chart is just a width and height in pixels. Multiply them for the total, then divide by one million for the megapixel figure:

$$\text{MP} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height}}{1{,}000{,}000}$$

For a 1440p mode, \(2560 \times 1440 = 3{,}686{,}400\) px, or 3.69 MP. The aspect ratio is the same two numbers reduced to their simplest form, so 2560:1440 becomes 16:9. The horizontal pixel count also explains the nicknames: "4K" refers to a width of roughly 4,000 px, while "1080p" names the height.

Camera Resolution and Image Quality

Camera resolution sets how much detail a frame can hold, but it does not guarantee image quality on its own. More pixels help when you crop, print large formats or view footage on big screens, yet sharpness and clarity also depend on the optics, light and the CMOS sensor behind them. A small image sensor squeezed to its top mode often looks softer than a larger one at a lower setting, which is why pixel totals alone are a weak measure of camera quality. So read the chart's MP column as a ceiling on detail, not a score: image sensors reach it only in good light, and photos for printing expose the gap fastest.

4K vs 1080p: Full HD and Ultra HD Compared

The three tiers most webcams advertise are:

  • Standard high definition (720p): 1280 by 720, about 0.9 MP.
  • Full high definition (1080p), sold as Full HD or as an FHD webcam: 1920 pixels wide by 1080 pixels tall, about 2.1 MP.
  • 4K ultra-high definition, or Ultra HD: 3840 × 2160, about 8.3 MP.

The "p" stands for progressive scan: every line of each frame is drawn in one pass rather than in alternating halves. 4K resolution matches what most current TVs, computer monitors and other display devices show natively, but on a call your image usually fills only part of someone's screen.

Video Resolution, Frame Rate and Bandwidth

Video resolution is only half of the picture; frame rate, measured in frames per second (fps), decides how smooth motion looks. 30 frames is normal for talking heads, and 60 makes movement noticeably smoother at the cost of a bigger file size. Both multiply the data your network has to carry. Uncompressed, a 1920 × 1080 feed at 30 frames in 8-bit 4:2:0 colour is about 746 Mbps; the same at 3840 × 2160 is roughly 2,986 Mbps, which is why every webcam compresses its output before it reaches your internet connection.

  • 1280 × 720 at 30 frames: about 332 Mbps raw.
  • 1920 × 1080 at 30 frames: about 746 Mbps raw.
  • 1920 × 1080 at 60 frames: about 1,493 Mbps raw.
  • 3840 × 2160 at 30 frames: about 2,986 Mbps raw.

After compression, the bandwidth you need still scales with those ratios, so your upload data transfer rate caps what you can send for video streaming, live streams or recording.

Video Conferencing Limits and CPU and GPU Load

Most video conferencing apps cap outgoing video calls at 1080p or lower, so a 4K feed is downscaled before anyone sees it, and Zoom or Twitch apply their own downscaling when your connection dips. Encoding high-resolution footage also leans on your CPU and GPU; on an older machine, dropping to 1080p can steady a stuttering video call.

Choosing a 1080p Webcam or 4K Webcam: Field of View and Lens

For everyday calls, a 1080p webcam is the sensible default: platforms rarely send more, and it is far kinder to bandwidth than a 4K webcam. A content creator who crops in, records tutorials or reuses footage gains more from 4K. Whatever you pick, an external webcam usually beats a laptop's built-in webcam. Also check the field of view: a wide-angle lens around 90° spreads the same 1920 × 1080 grid over two people or a whiteboard, so each face gets fewer px than at 65-78°.

Glass Lens vs Plastic Lens

A glass lens resolves finer details and resists scratches, which matters once you move from 1280 × 720 to the larger rows of the chart. A plastic lens is cheaper and fine for the smaller modes, but it can cap real sharpness below the sensor's rated resolution.

Find Supported Resolutions With a Resolution Test

A spec sheet lists the headline mode, not every mode your camera accepts. A resolution test in the browser asks the camera for each standard in the chart and reports which ones it actually delivers; some tools add a brute-force method that also finds non-standard resolutions.

Checking Maximum Resolution and FPS

  1. Open a webcam resolution tester and allow camera access in your browser.
  2. Note the default resolution the browser picks, which is often lower than your camera's best.
  3. Run the scan to find the maximum resolution, the minimum resolution and the fps for each mode.
  4. If you use multiple webcams, select each one in turn and export the results.

Why Picture Quality Looks Grainy, Noisy or Blurry

Poor picture quality is not always a resolution problem. First compare the mode the test reports with the chart: another app holding the camera can force it down to 640 × 480. If the mode is right, poor lighting makes the image grainy and noisy and can lower fps, and a smudged lens leaves video blurry at any setting.

faq.question: Does higher webcam resolution always mean better image quality?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Image quality depends on a combination of factors including sensor size, lens quality, and image processing software. A lower-resolution webcam with a high-quality sensor and glass lens can outperform a higher-resolution model with inferior components. Resolution is just one piece of the overall image quality puzzle.

faq.question: What is the difference between resolution and megapixels in a webcam?
faq.answer: Resolution refers to the pixel dimensions of the image (e.g. 1920×1080), while megapixels is the total pixel count expressed in millions (1920×1080 = ~2.07 MP). They are related but not identical — a 2K webcam at 2560×1440 has 3.69 MP, while a 4K webcam at 3840×2160 has 8.29 MP. Manufacturers sometimes round or market these numbers differently, so always check the actual pixel dimensions.

faq.question: What webcam resolution is best for video calls and conferencing?
faq.answer: 1080p (Full HD) at 30 fps is the sweet spot for most video conferencing platforms like Zoom, Teams, and Google Meet. It delivers clear, sharp video without demanding excessive upload bandwidth. 720p is acceptable for standard calls, while 4K is rarely necessary and may be downscaled by conferencing platforms anyway.

faq.question: How does frame rate affect webcam video quality?
faq.answer: Frame rate (fps) determines how smooth the video appears. 30 fps is the standard for most webcams and video calls, producing natural-looking motion. 60 fps results in noticeably smoother video, which is useful for streaming or gaming captures, but requires roughly double the bandwidth and processing power. 15 fps may appear choppy but is sometimes used in low-bandwidth situations.

faq.question: What upload speed do I need for streaming at 1080p or 4K?
faq.answer: For 1080p H.264 video at 30 fps, a stable upload speed of at least 4–6 Mbps is recommended. For 4K streaming, you typically need 15–25 Mbps or more, depending on the codec and platform. It's wise to have a connection that can sustain roughly 1.5× the target bitrate to account for network fluctuations.

faq.question: What is the difference between a glass lens and a plastic lens in a webcam?
faq.answer: Glass lenses generally produce sharper, more accurate images with less distortion and chromatic aberration, especially at the edges of the frame. Plastic lenses are lighter and cheaper to manufacture but can introduce softness and color fringing. For professional video calls or streaming, a glass lens webcam is usually worth the additional cost.

faq.question: Does a wider field of view (FOV) mean a better webcam?
faq.answer: Not necessarily — it depends on your use case. A wider FOV captures more of the room, which is useful for group calls or whiteboard presentations, but it can also distort your face if you're sitting close to the camera. A narrower FOV (around 65–78°) often looks more flattering for solo video calls, providing a more natural, portrait-like perspective.

faq.question: What do auto exposure, auto focus, and auto white balance do on a webcam?
faq.answer: Auto Exposure adjusts the shutter speed and gain to maintain consistent brightness as lighting conditions change. Auto Focus continuously sharpens the image as you move or your environment shifts. Auto White Balance corrects color temperature so that whites appear neutral under different light sources (daylight, fluorescent, LED). While these settings are convenient, they can sometimes over-correct — manual controls give more consistent results in stable environments.

h1: Microphone Spectrum Analyzer: Free Mic Quality Test
subtitle: Click Start Microphone on this microphone spectrum analyzer to see your live spectrum and Dominant Frequency.

card.fields_html:
Microphone Quality & Spectrum

Live frequency spectrum, logarithmic axis (20 Hz – ~20 kHz)

20 Hz200 Hz2 kHz20 kHz
Click Start Microphone and allow access when your browser asks.

Readings

—Dominant Frequency
—Noise Floor
—Mains Hum
—Sample Rate

Stay silent for 2 seconds while measuring — this captures your room's background noise level for comparison.

Why Processing Is Disabled

This test deliberately requests your microphone with echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain control all turned off. Those features are on by default in most calling apps, but they actively reshape the frequency spectrum — leaving them on here would measure your browser's processing, not your microphone.

Mains hum shows up as a spike at exactly 50 Hz (most of the world) or 60 Hz (North America and parts of Asia) — usually from a nearby power supply, unshielded cable, or ground loop.

content_html:
Your microphone quality and spectrum check starts the moment you press Start: this free microphone spectrum analyzer turns live audio from your microphone into a real-time FFT graph of every frequency between 20 Hz and 20 kHz. You see which frequencies it captures strongly, where it fades, and how much bass, mid and treble loudness it actually captures — the same view sound engineers use for mixing and mastering, without installing anything.

How to Run a Mic Test on the Frequency Spectrum

A mic test here takes about ten seconds and runs entirely in your browser through the Web Audio API. Nothing is uploaded or stored: your audio is analysed on your own device and discarded straight away, so no recording ever leaves your computer. This online frequency analyser needs only a working input and permission to use it.

  1. Click Start and allow microphone access when the browser asks.
  2. Choose the right input — a built-in mic, a USB headset or an audio interface — from the device list.
  3. Speak, sing or play a steady sound and watch the frequencies fill the frequency spectrum.
  4. Stay silent for five seconds to see the hiss your setup produces on its own.
  5. Switch to the spectrogram to watch how your frequencies change over time, and hover any peak on the spectrum display to read its exact value.

To check playback instead of your microphone — a music app or a video in another tab, or a reference track for mixing — use the browser's tab-capture option and tick "Share tab audio"; where that isn't supported, upload an audio file instead.

Microphone Access, Gain and FFT Size Settings

FFT size sets how finely the frequency axis is sliced: larger sizes separate close tones but react more slowly. Gain lifts a quiet signal so it fills the display, without changing the capsule itself. Smoothing averages successive frames so the trace stops flickering; turn it down when you are hunting short clicks. Leave the frequency axis in its default log view unless you are checking electronics, because a linear scale crams everything below 1 kHz into a sliver on the left and makes audio work much harder to read.

Reading the Logarithmic Scale and Peak Frequency

The horizontal axis runs from 20 Hz (bass, left) to 20 kHz (treble, right) on a logarithmic scale, so every octave takes the same width — the way you hear pitch and the standard for mixing. The vertical axis shows amplitude in dBFS, decibels relative to digital full scale: zero is the loudest value the converter can store, and everything below it is negative. Bar height is loudness. The tallest bar is the peak frequency; hover over it to read its value in Hz, then look for other tall peak frequencies at whole-number multiples of it.

What the Sound Spectrum Analyzer Measures

A microphone records pressure changes over time — a waveform in the time domain. The sound spectrum analyzer runs a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on short slices of that audio signal, using the Web Audio API, to move it into the frequency domain, where each bar shows how much energy sits at one frequency. The real-time result covers every frequency between 20 Hz and 20 kHz and tells you what your microphone actually hears: which frequencies it captures strongly, which it misses, and what unwanted sound rides along with every word.

FFT Bins, Frequency Resolution and Sample Rate

An FFT splits the audio band from 0 Hz up to half the sample rate into equal slices called bins. The width of each bin is your frequency resolution, and the length of audio each frame needs is the window:

$$\Delta f = \frac{f_s}{N} \qquad T = \frac{N}{f_s}$$

where \(f_s\) is the sampling frequency in Hz and \(N\) is the number of FFT points. Take a typical USB headset running at 44,100 Hz with an FFT size of 2,048: each bin is 44,100 ÷ 2,048 = 21.53 Hz wide and each frame covers 46.4 ms. Good spectrum analysis is always that compromise between detail and speed:

FFT pointsBin width at 48 kHzWindow length
1,02446.88 Hz21.3 ms
2,04823.44 Hz42.7 ms
4,09611.72 Hz85.3 ms
8,1925.86 Hz170.7 ms
16,3842.93 Hz341.3 ms

Small sizes suit speech and fast transients; large ones separate two tones a few hertz apart. That is why every FFT analyser lets you change it.

RMS Level, Crest Factor and Clipping

The meters beside the graph summarise the signal over time. Peak is the single loudest sample; RMS level is the average power and tracks perceived loudness more closely; the crest factor is the gap between them in dB. Say a spoken line reads a peak of −3.2 dBFS and an RMS level of −17.6 dBFS: that 14.4 dB gap is typical of natural, uncompressed dialogue. Values of 6 dB or less point to heavy compression or a limiter, while a very dynamic performance can run well above 20 dB. If the peak hold touches zero, the input is clipping — lower the input level until peaks stay several dB below full scale, because clipped audio carries distortion you cannot remove later. The VU meters and the oscilloscope also reveal DC offset, a waveform pushed off its centre line.

Spectral Centroid, Dominant Frequency and Note Detection

The dominant frequency is the loudest bin, and note detection maps it to the nearest note (A4 = 440 Hz) with an offset in cents. That helps with tuning instruments and, even more, with naming a noise: a 60 Hz tone reads as B1, 49 cents flat. Because a harmonic can be louder than the fundamental, better tools search for the fundamental frequency behind the overtones rather than trusting the tallest bar, so you get the right note in the right octave. The spectral centroid is the amplitude-weighted average frequency — one number for brightness. If it falls sharply when you swap mics on the same singer, the second microphone has a darker timbre.

Judging Microphone Quality and Spectrum Bands

To judge a microphone, record the same spoken line at the same distance and read the spectrum band by band. A good vocal model shows a smooth curve through the lower and middle bands, a gentle lift in the presence region for clarity, and no spikes at fixed frequencies once you stop talking. The table maps each band of the audio spectrum to what it adds and what a problem looks like.

BandRangeWhat it addsWhat a problem looks like
Sub bass20 Hz–60 HzWeight you feel more than hearRumble from desks, stands or traffic
Bass60–250 HzWarmth of vocals, body of a kick drumBoom and muddiness up close
Low mid250–500 HzFullness of speechBoxiness from a small, bare room
Mid500 Hz–2 kHzFundamental of most vocals and instrumentsNasal or honky tone
Upper mid2–4 kHzConsonants, where hearing is most sensitiveHarshness on cheap capsules
Presence4–6 kHzArticulation and clarityDull, muffled words if this band drops away
Brilliance6–12 kHzSparkle on cymbals and hi-hatSpitty "s" sounds
Air12 kHz–20 kHzOpenness and room soundSelf-noise sitting flat across the top of the audio band

Noise Floor and Background Noise

Mute yourself and the trace that remains is the noise floor: the capsule's self-noise, preamp hiss and the room's background noise combined. A healthy setup leaves a low, flat line. A broad hump in the bass points to traffic or ventilation, and a raised, even layer across the treble points to a noisy preamp or an input level set too high. Compare that floor with your speaking level in the online frequency analyser — the further your voice sits above it, the cleaner the audio. If the floor rises as you raise the input level, the problem lives early in the signal chain, not in the room.

Mains Hum at 50 Hz and 60 Hz

Mains hum shows up in the frequency analyser as a narrow spike that stays put whatever you say — 60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in Europe and much of Asia — with each harmonic stacked at whole multiples above it. Electrical hum almost always comes from the cable path, not the capsule: a ground loop between computer and interface, an unbalanced lead running past a power supply, or poor shielding. Fix it with balanced connections, a single shared power strip or a ground loop isolator, then rerun the test and confirm the spike is gone.

Proximity Effect and Sibilance

Two capsule effects show up clearly among the frequencies. Proximity effect is the bass boost directional mics add as you move closer: record a phrase at 30 cm and again at 5 cm, and the bass energy below 200 Hz climbs while the spectral centroid falls. Sibilance appears on the spectrogram as bright bursts between 5 and 9 kHz on every "s" and "t". If either is excessive, change position or angle before reaching for mixing EQ — a mic placed slightly off-axis often tames both.

Chasing Audiobook Hum with the Online Frequency Checker

I'm about to record a narration sample for an audiobook platform that follows ACX's published specs: RMS between −23 and −18 dB, peaks no higher than −3 dB, and a noise floor no louder than −60 dB RMS. The chain is a second-hand dynamic mic into a two-channel interface at 48 kHz, and the decision is simple: record tonight, or fix something first?

I set the FFT size to 2,048 points, read a test paragraph, then sit silent for ten seconds of room tone. The readings:

  • Speech RMS −21.7 dBFS, peak −4.6 dBFS — both inside the window.
  • Room tone RMS −64.2 dBFS, a gap of −21.7 − (−64.2) = 42.5 dB, so the −60 dB floor rule passes.
  • A narrow spike the peak readout labels 70.3 Hz, at −61.3 dBFS, with smaller spikes above it.

That 70.3 Hz label nearly fooled me. At 48,000 ÷ 2,048 each bin is 23.44 Hz wide, and 60 Hz sits 2.56 bins up, so its energy lands in the 70.3 Hz bin and reads about 0.8 dB low. Raising the FFT size to 4,096 moves the label to 58.6 Hz, with neighbours at 117 and 176 Hz: 60 Hz mains hum and its harmonics, plain as day on the frequency spectrum. The RMS figure alone would have passed this take, yet anyone on headphones would hear that tone in every pause.

The laptop and interface are on different wall sockets, so I move both onto one power strip and rerun with nothing else changed:

ReadingBeforeAfter one power strip
60 Hz spike−61.3 dBFS−79.5 dBFS
Room tone RMS−64.2 dBFS−71.6 dBFS
Speech-to-room-tone gap42.5 dB49.9 dB

One cable change bought 7.4 dB of quieter floor and pushed the hum down 18.2 dB. My judgement: on this kind of check, the number to watch is the hum spike against your speech, not the overall floor, because a pure tone carries little energy but stands out in silence. I'll record tonight, and rerun the test after any cabling change, since a new USB hub can bring the loop straight back.

Microphone Frequency Response and the Hearing Range

Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the hearing range shrinks in the top octave with age. A microphone's frequency response describes how evenly it captures those frequencies. Many vocal models deliberately trim the deep bass and the top of the treble, below 80–100 Hz and above 15–16 kHz; that rolloff is fine for talking but shows clearly in a frequency analysis of music. To compare two mics, save the first as a reference trace, swap mics without moving anything, and read the gap between the two curves in the online frequency checker. A difference of a few dB is a change of character you can correct with EQ; a gap of 10 dB or more in one band is a real limit. Your own mic colours every reading, so for speaker or room work use a flat, calibrated measurement microphone.

Pink Noise, Sweeps and Room Modes

The frequency analyser can also judge the room and speakers around you. Play pink noise — equal energy per octave — from a tone generator through a speaker, put the capsule at the listening position, and peaks and nulls in the bass reveal room modes. White noise has equal energy per hertz and looks tilted upward on the display; a sine wave tests one frequency; a log sweep from 20 Hz to 20 kHz exposes resonances and cancellations, a quick check of room acoustics. The lowest axial mode is the speed of sound divided by twice the room length: a 5.2 m room gives 343 ÷ 10.4 ≈ 33 Hz. Keep levels low, because sweeps at high volume can damage tweeters.

Octave Bands and Z Weighting

Octave bands group the spectrum's frequencies into proportional slices: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is almost exactly ten octaves, so a full-octave view gives about ten bars and a 1/3 octave view about thirty-one. The weighting setting changes how they are summed: Z is flat, A mimics how quiet sounds are heard and trims bass, and C weighting stays flatter in the bass for loud or impact sounds. None of this turns a browser into a calibrated SPL meter — treat readings as relative, not absolute.

Spectrogram and Waveform Views in the Online Frequency Analyser

The bar graph shows one instant; the spectrogram shows time. It scrolls left to right with frequencies running bottom to top and colour showing amplitude, so a steady tone draws a horizontal line, a room resonance leaves a streak that lingers after you stop, and a sung phrase appears as stacked harmonics that bend with your pitch. The waveform oscilloscope shows the raw real-time audio trace instead, which is the quickest way to spot clipped flat tops, while the VU meters track level. When you find something worth keeping, freeze the display, save a screenshot, or export the spectrum as CSV to open in a spreadsheet — this online frequency analyser keeps all of it on your device.

Mid/Side Stereo and Mono Audio Checks

With a stereo pair, the mid/side view splits the signal into what both channels share and what differs between them. A strong side signal means a wide image; a near-empty side means your recording will hold up in mono. For a single USB model, the side channel should be almost silent — if it isn't, one channel may be faulty or out of phase.

Leq, L10 and L90 Noise Sessions

For longer checks, a session logs levels over time. Leq is the energy-average level for the whole run, L10 the level exceeded 10% of the time (the loud moments) and L90 the level exceeded 90% of the time — effectively your room's background floor. A minute suits steady noise such as an air conditioner; give a busy room several minutes so the background reading settles, then export the log. A wide gap between the two tells you the noise comes and goes, which matters when you pick a time to record.

Who Uses a Real-Time Spectrum Analyser

Anyone who needs to see audio rather than guess at it. A real-time spectrum analyser in the browser works as a quick frequency checker for:

  • Streaming and podcast setups — confirm your headset or USB mic is clean, free of hum and not overloading before you go live.
  • Music production — check vocal and instrument recordings, low-end balance and EQ decisions while mixing.
  • Microphone testing — compare two mics, or one mic at different distances, against a saved reference.
  • Speaker and room checks — find room resonances and speaker rolloff with a test signal.
  • Broadcast and voice work — catch sub-20 Hz rumble, hiss and harsh esses before delivery.
  • Learning audio — sing a note, check your tuning, and watch the fundamental and harmonics appear on the spectrogram.

Sound engineers still use dedicated hardware for certified measurements, but for everyday audio analysis this free frequency analyser and online frequency checker cover every microphone quality and spectrum check that matters.

faq.question: What does a microphone spectrum analyzer show?
faq.answer: It splits the sound your mic picks up into its frequencies with a Fast Fourier Transform and shows how loud each one is, from 20 Hz bass on the left to 20 kHz treble on the right. Taller bars mean more energy at that frequency.

faq.question: Is my audio recorded or uploaded?
faq.answer: No. The analysis runs in your browser through the Web Audio API, and the audio is processed on your device and discarded. Nothing is sent to a server.

faq.question: Which FFT size should I choose?
faq.answer: Smaller sizes react faster and suit speech and transients; larger sizes give finer frequency resolution for separating close tones such as hum and a bass note. Resolution is the sample rate divided by the FFT size, so 4,096 points at 48 kHz gives about 11.7 Hz per bin.

faq.question: How do I find 50 Hz or 60 Hz mains hum?
faq.answer: Stay silent and look for a narrow spike that does not move at 50 Hz (Europe, most of Asia) or 60 Hz (North America), often with weaker spikes at whole multiples. Balanced cables, a shared power strip or a ground loop isolator usually remove it.

faq.question: What is the difference between A, C and Z weighting?
faq.answer: Z is flat and treats every frequency equally. A follows how the ear hears quiet sounds and reads bass and extreme treble lower. C stays much flatter in the bass and suits loud or impact noise. None of them turns a browser into a calibrated sound level meter.

faq.question: What do Leq, L10 and L90 mean?
faq.answer: Leq is the energy-average level over a session, L10 the level exceeded 10% of the time (the loud moments) and L90 the level exceeded 90% of the time, which is effectively your background noise floor. A large gap between L10 and L90 means the noise comes and goes.

faq.question: What do peak, RMS and crest factor tell me about my mic?
faq.answer: Peak is the loudest single sample and shows how close you are to clipping. RMS is the average power and tracks perceived loudness. Crest factor is peak minus RMS: a high value means natural, dynamic audio, a low value means heavy compression.

h1: Frequency Sweep Test: Play Sine Sweeps from 20 Hz to 20 kHz
subtitle: Click Start Sweep on this frequency sweep test to sweep 20Hz to 20kHz and catch any dropouts or rattles.

card.fields_html:
Frequency Sweep Test

Sweeps 20 Hz to 20 kHz to reveal dropouts, rattles and resonances

—
Turn your volume down before starting. A sweep played at high volume can damage tweeters and small speakers — start quiet and raise it gradually if needed.

Sweep Settings

30%

Jump to a Frequency

Report an exact frequency where you hear a problem

Dragging this plays a steady tone at that exact frequency — pauses the sweep automatically.

content_html:
Press play and the frequency sweep test above glides one pure tone through every pitch your audio gear can make, so you hear where the sound swells, thins or buzzes. Unlike fixed sweep test tones or separate test tones, these sweeps cover 20 Hz to 20 kHz (or any band in Hz and kHz) in seconds, and weak spots in your playback chain stand out the moment the level jumps.

How the Frequency Sweep Test Works

This frequency sweep generator produces one continuous signal whose frequency rises or falls between two points you set. The sweeper runs in Chrome, Safari and Firefox, so the frequency sweep tool needs no download. With one tone at a time, the sweep generator gives each frequency the full signal level.

Setting the Start Frequency and Stop Frequency

Enter a start frequency, a stop frequency and a duration in seconds, then pick a waveform: sine for clean checks, or square, sawtooth and triangle, which add harmonics. Start volume and end volume boxes let the signal fade in or out.

Log Sweep or Linear Sweep Test Sound

A log sweep spends equal time on every octave, the way your ears hear pitch. A linear sweep adds the same hertz each second, so it races through the low end; its energy spreads like white noise, while a logarithmic one sounds closer to pink. The logarithmic frequency at time \(t\) is:

$$f(t) = f_{1} \times \left(\frac{f_{2}}{f_{1}}\right)^{t/T}$$

Take 25 Hz to 12,800 Hz over 18 seconds: \(12{,}800 \div 25 = 512 = 2^{9}\), so 9 octaves of 2 s each, passing 566 Hz at 9 s. The linear version climbs 709.7 Hz per second and is already at 6,412 Hz halfway through.

OctaveLogarithmic (s)Linear (s)
25–50 Hz2.00.035
100–200 Hz2.00.141
400–800 Hz2.00.564
1.6–3.2 kHz2.02.254
6.4–12.8 kHz2.09.018

Below 200 Hz the log run plays for 6 s, the linear one for 0.25 s, so use the log version by ear.

What a Sine Sweep Reveals About Frequency Response and Room Modes

As the sine sweep rises, loudness should change smoothly. Any jump reveals the frequency response of your audio system at your listening location:

  • Peaks: a boost from room modes or other resonant frequencies of the listening room.
  • Dips: holes where reflections cancel (anti-resonances).
  • Rattling: furniture or trim buzzing at its resonances.
  • Fade-out: the speaker's limit at either end.

No real room gives a flat response, so look for sharp, narrow changes, not gentle slopes.

Bass and Subwoofer Test Sound

The low frequency band is where rooms misbehave most. Sweep 20–120 Hz slowly to hear where your subwoofer becomes audible and where bass booms. If the hand-off to your loudspeakers dips, flip the sub's phase switch and rerun. Full-bandwidth speakers benefit too.

Hearing the Test Tone at a Safe Level

Run each pass at a comfortable volume: the test tone puts all its energy at one pitch as it climbs, which can harm your hearing or a tweeter. As the signal rises through the upper mids it seems louder than it is (the Fletcher-Munson, or equal loudness, effect), so judge only sudden jumps along the way. A raspy edge that appears partway up means harmonic distortion from an overdriven amp, which music tends to hide.

Tracking Down a Bass Boom With the Frequency Sweep Tool

A new subwoofer sits in the corner of a 4.37 m by 3.62 m den, and one note in every film booms while the next sounds hollow. The goal is to decide whether to move the sub or just change its crossover, and the answer comes in under a minute: a boom at about 39 Hz, the room's own length mode, not a fault in the sub.

Before pressing play, I predict where the trouble should sit. The first axial mode of a room is the speed of sound over twice its length: \(343 \div (2 \times 4.37) = 39.24\) Hz. The width gives \(343 \div 7.24 = 47.38\) Hz, and the second length mode doubles to 78.49 Hz.

Into the frequency sweep tool go a 28 Hz start, a 179.2 Hz stop and a 16-second duration, sine, logarithmic. That range is 2.68 octaves, so each octave gets almost 6 seconds, slow enough to hear a single mode. From the listening seat, the swell arrives about 2.9 s in, which the log formula puts at 39.2 Hz; a softer bump follows at 4.5 s (47 Hz), then a dip near 8.9 s.

EventPredictedHeard at
Length mode39.24 Hz2.9 s
Width mode47.38 Hz4.5 s
Second length mode78.49 Hz8.9 s

For a sensitivity check I rerun the same band over 6 seconds. The window within 3 Hz of the mode (36.25–42.25 Hz) shrinks from 1.32 s to 0.50 s and the boom turns into a blink that is easy to miss, which is why a quick sweep can make a bad room sound fine.

The caveat that matters: the second length mode lands only 1.5 Hz below the common 80 Hz crossover, so the dip at 8.9 s may be the hand-off between sub and mains, not the room. Flipping the sub's phase and rerunning separates the two; if the dip moves, it was the crossover. The 39 Hz peak won't move with any setting, so the next step is sliding the sub 60 cm out of the corner and sweeping again from the same seat. Moving your chair changes what you hear as much as moving the sub, so keep the seat fixed between runs.

Sweep Measurements With a Spectrum Analyzer

For an objective audio measurement, record the signal with a microphone. On a real time analyzer or spectrum analyzer, turn on peak hold so the whole audio spectrum builds up in one pass; an FFT analyzer with linear bins pairs with the linear version. Measurement software derives the impulse response from a swept sine, then the amplitude response, phase response and distortion. A time window removes reflections, and on a speaker driver the same test can plot impedance. Phones with no audio input play a stored signal after a short trigger tone so the analyzer can sync.

Glide Sweep, Chirp and Stepped Sweep

A glide sweep, or chirp, moves continuously, so a short one loses no resolution. A stepped sweep jumps between fixed points and waits for settling at each. Hold the frequency and step the amplitude instead for an amplitude sweep, the standard linearity test.

Sine Sweeps Compared With Pink Noise and Other Test Signals

Sine sweeps put full power into one frequency at a time, so they stay clear of background sound and pin down a single resonance. Pink noise plays everything at once with equal energy per octave, which suits quick A/B checks. Other test signals fill gaps: a short sweep tone for subwoofers, a full sine sweep for whole-range checks, or a sweep signal 6 dB below full scale for safe gain staging.

Saving Sweep Tones for Your Audio Equipment

To test audio equipment away from a browser, such as a car stereo, save the sweep tone generator output as a lossless WAV rather than MP3, since MP3 encoding can trim the extremes of the audible range.

faq.question: What does a frequency sweep test check?
faq.answer: It plays one tone that moves steadily through the frequency range, so you can hear where your speakers, headphones or room boost or cut certain notes. Sudden peaks, dips, rattles or a fade-out at either end show where the playback chain is uneven.

faq.question: Should I use a linear or a logarithmic sweep?
faq.answer: Use a logarithmic (exponential) sweep when listening by ear, because it gives every octave the same time, the way your ears hear pitch. A linear sweep rushes through the bass in a fraction of a second and spends most of its time in the treble, which suits a linear FFT analyzer.

faq.question: Which waveform should I choose?
faq.answer: Choose sine for response checks, since it contains a single frequency at a time. Square, sawtooth and triangle waves add harmonics above the fundamental, which is useful for hearing distortion or buzzes but makes the response harder to judge.

faq.question: How can I find room modes and resonances with a sweep?
faq.answer: Sweep the bass range slowly from your usual listening position and note where the level suddenly swells or drops. Swells are usually room modes or resonances, dips are cancellations, and buzzing at one note points to something in the room rattling.

faq.question: Why do some frequencies sound louder even if my system is flat?
faq.answer: Your ears are more sensitive in the upper midrange, an effect described by the Fletcher-Munson equal loudness curves. Ignore gentle, broad changes in loudness and look only for sharp, narrow peaks and dips.

faq.question: Is a frequency sweep safe for my ears and speakers?
faq.answer: Start at a low volume and only raise it to a comfortable level. A sweep concentrates all its energy at one frequency at a time, so a loud high-frequency tone can damage your hearing or a tweeter.

faq.question: How is a sine sweep different from pink noise?
faq.answer: A sine sweep plays one frequency at a time with the full signal level, so it stands out above background noise and pinpoints individual resonances. Pink noise plays all frequencies at once with equal energy per octave, which is better for quick A/B comparisons and real-time analyzer calibration.

card.tool_warning: This is not a medical hearing test. It's a rough, informal estimate for fun — the result depends entirely on your speakers or headphones, which vary hugely and often can't reproduce the highest frequencies at all regardless of your actual hearing. If you have genuine concerns about your hearing, see an audiologist.

content_html:
Wondering whether you or a loved one is missing more than you realise? This online hearing test plays beeps and spoken words and, in about 3 minutes, shows how well each ear is hearing. Treat it as a hearing screener and the first step in your hearing journey, not a verdict. Take the hearing test online with headphones for the cleanest result.

How the Free Online Hearing Test Works

Most versions of this online test follow the same pattern: answer a few questions, then follow the on-screen prompts from the comfort of your home. No email address is needed, and it takes a few minutes.

Pure Tones From Low-Pitched to High-Pitched

A frequency test plays beeps one ear at a time, from a low-pitched hum near 250 Hz to a high-pitched whistle near 8,000 Hz, getting quieter across several volume levels. The quietest sound you catch is your threshold for that pitch. Testing your ears individually matters, because loss often starts in one ear.

Speech in Background Noise

Other checks, like the digits test from one independent UK charity, play spoken numbers over white noise. Plenty of people pass a tone check yet struggle to follow a voice in a busy room.

Before You Start the Hearing Screener

Setup decides how much you can trust any hearing test online.

Headphones and a Quiet Place

Wear headphones or earphones, not device speakers or built-in speakers, so each beep reaches one ear. Find a quiet place, or a quiet area with no TV running, and set your sound to its highest level. If you wear hearing aids, remove them first. That gives the most accurate results.

Who Should Skip This Hearing Test

These checks suit adults aged 18 and over with no existing diagnosis. If you live with tinnitus, ringing can mask the quietest beeps, so a clinic visit is the better route.

Reading Your Online Hearing Test Results

Most tools give broad bands such as good hearing or some loss. A pure-tone check gives an indication of your hearing ability at each pitch.

Pure-Tone Average and the WHO Hearing Loss Grades

Clinicians summarise each ear with the pure-tone average (PTA):

$$\text{PTA} = \frac{T_{500} + T_{1000} + T_{2000} + T_{4000}}{4}$$

Ear500 Hz1,000 Hz2,000 Hz4,000 HzPTAGrade
Left1520304527.5 dBMild
Right1010152515 dBNormal

The World Health Organization grades a PTA under 20 dB as normal and 20 to under 35 dB as mild hearing loss. Over 35 dB in the better ear counts as disabling hearing loss, and severity climbs to 95 dB and beyond for people who are deaf. In this example the left ear is mild, and the 20 dB gap at 4,000 Hz is worth showing a clinician.

Why a Hearing Age Can Be Misleading

Some sites turn your score into a hearing age. That's misleading: loss affects every stage of life, and its cause may be loud music, infection or genetics rather than the years.

Running a Hearing Check After a Season of Band Rehearsals

I drum in a covers band, and after eight weeks of two-hour rehearsals my right ear, the one nearest the ride cymbal, feels dull in the car home. The decision I want to make is simple: is this worth a clinic visit, or just a reason to finally wear earplugs? I run the tone test on this page before deciding. The answer comes back as a right-ear pure-tone average of 32.5 dB, mild loss and an ear-to-ear gap big enough to book a proper test.

I use closed-back headphones, sit in the spare room with the door shut, and start the pure-tone check described above the evening after a rehearsal. The right ear's quietest beeps come in at 20, 25, 35 and 50 dB across 500, 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 Hz; the left at 15, 15, 20 and 30 dB. I add them by hand to check the screen: 130 ÷ 4 = 32.5 dB on the right, 80 ÷ 4 = 20 dB on the left. Both sit inside the WHO mild band of 20 to under 35 dB, but the right ear is 20 dB worse at 4,000 Hz, the pitch where noise damage usually shows first.

Then I rerun it after 36 quiet hours:

Right ear500 Hz1,000 Hz2,000 Hz4,000 HzPTA
Evening after rehearsal2025355032.5 dB
After 36 quiet hours2020304528.75 dB

That 3.75 dB recovery is a temporary threshold shift, and it's the trap here: testing straight after loud sound overstates the loss. The opposite trap matters more. Because most online tools step in 5 dB, the first run sat just two one-pitch steps from the 35 dB moderate line, so one misheard beep can move the grade. I'd trust the pattern, one ear worse at high pitches on both runs, far more than either average.

My judgement: the 4,000 Hz gap is the number to watch, not the average. Next step is an audiologist appointment with both screenshots, plus earplugs at rehearsal (NIOSH allows just 15 minutes at 100 dBA), and a retest on this page in three months to see whether that 4,000 Hz gap holds steady.

Signs of Hearing Loss a Hearing Check Can Confirm

  • Difficulty hearing conversations in restaurants
  • Asking people to repeat themselves
  • Turning up the volume on the television or radio
  • Struggling to follow a voice on the phone
  • Listening fatigue from trying to concentrate

Any of these hearing challenges is reason to run a free hearing check and keep the outcome for next year.

Why an Early Hearing Evaluation Protects Your Hearing Health

Untreated loss pulls people away from social settings, and that isolation is linked to anxiety, frustration and poorer mental health. Studies also tie mild loss to a higher risk of dementia. Spotting it early gives you time to treat it before your well-being suffers and you feel isolated. A screen like the one on this page is the quickest way to catch that early change: save your scores and repeat it once a year.

Online Test vs a Professional Hearing Test

A 3-minute hearing test can't replace an in-person test. It can't control your equipment or tell the type of hearing loss, so it's never a medical diagnosis. Only a full hearing evaluation can, and it takes longer than three minutes.

Book an Appointment After Your Online Hearing Test

If one ear scores worse or any loss shows, book an appointment with a hearing care professional at a hearing clinic. Bring a screenshot of your scores to plan next steps. Hearing care teams can also check for earwax.

Where Hearing Aids Fit In

If the clinic confirms a loss, modern devices amplify the pitches you're missing. An early screen shortens the years many people wait.

faq.question: Is this online hearing test free?
faq.answer: Yes. It costs nothing, needs no email address and takes about three minutes from the comfort of your home.

faq.question: What do I need to take the test?
faq.answer: A quiet place, a pair of headphones or earphones, and your device volume turned up before you start. If you wear hearing aids, take them out first.

faq.question: Can I take the hearing test with device speakers?
faq.answer: You can, but speakers play to both ears at once, so the result only reflects your better ear. Headphones test each ear individually and give more accurate results.

faq.question: Can an online hearing test replace a professional hearing test?
faq.answer: No. It is a screening, not a medical diagnosis. Only an in-person evaluation by a hearing care professional can tell the cause, type and severity of hearing loss.

faq.question: What does the pure-tone average mean?
faq.answer: It is the average of the quietest beeps you heard at 500, 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 Hz. Under 20 dB is normal on the WHO scale, and 20 to under 35 dB is mild hearing loss.

faq.question: What are the signs of hearing loss?
faq.answer: Common signs include trouble following conversations, asking people to repeat themselves, turning up the TV or radio, difficulty on the phone and feeling tired after concentrating to listen.

faq.question: Why doesn't this test give me a hearing age?
faq.answer: A hearing age can be misleading, because hearing loss happens at every age and often has causes other than getting older. The test reports each ear's level and grade instead.

h1: Composition Grid: Free Rule of Thirds Grid Overlay
subtitle: Click Start Camera and toggle Rule of Thirds on this rule of thirds grid to check your framing live.

card.fields_html:
Composition Grid

Framing guides overlaid on your live feed — position yourself using the grid below

Your camera feed will appear here
Click Start Camera and allow access when your browser asks.

Guides

Toggle each on or off

Framing Tips

Eye level: aim to have your eyes sit on or near the upper third line, not the exact centre — this is the single biggest framing improvement most people can make.

Headroom: leave a small, even gap above your head rather than a large empty band — too much headroom pushes your face down and out of the frame's visual centre.

Safe area: keep your face and shoulders within the inner rectangle so nothing important gets cropped on displays that don't show the full frame edge-to-edge.

content_html:
Not sure whether your shot is framed well or just framed? Drop any image into this composition grid and it draws a rule of thirds grid, a golden-section phi layout or a diagonal guide on top, with the exact pixel position of every line and crossing. Think of it as a free grid generator that turns framing and placement from a hunch into something you can check on a photo before you publish it.

What a Composition Grid Shows You

The classic overlay is a 3x3 grid: two horizontal lines and two vertical lines split the picture into nine equal rectangles. The lines sit at one-third and two-thirds of the width and height, so each band is roughly 33.3% of the picture. Because the rectangles are equal parts of the picture, the grid works on any aspect ratio, from a 16:9 video still to a 4:5 social post. The grid lines themselves are only scaffolding for composition; what matters is where your subject lands against them, and whether it sits near the intersections.

Where the Intersection Points Fall

The four crossings are the intersection points, sometimes called power points. For an image W pixels wide and H pixels tall, the lines sit at:

$$x_1 = \frac{W}{3},\quad x_2 = \frac{2W}{3},\qquad y_1 = \frac{H}{3},\quad y_2 = \frac{2H}{3}$$

Place your focal point or main subject on one of these intersections, often the upper-right intersection when the person or object looks or moves to the left, and leave the rest of the picture to breathe.

How to Use the Rule of Thirds Tool

  1. Load a JPG, PNG or WebP image, or a still from your webcam. Nothing leaves your browser.
  2. Pick a grid: thirds, phi, diagonals or one of the other composition overlays.
  3. Set the line colour and opacity so the guide stays visible on bright and dark areas.
  4. Switch on the intersection markers and read the pixel positions in the results panel.
  5. Nudge your edit until the key element sits on a crossing, then save the result.

That is the whole workflow of a free rule of thirds grid: no signup, no upload, and the same rule of thirds generator logic your editing app uses.

Export a Printable Cropping Guide

You can export the lines alone as a transparent PNG and lay them over any picture in another app. Printed on acetate, the same printable sheet becomes a physical guide for prints, card designs or a canvas you are about to paint on.

Worked Example: Composition Grid Positions on an 18 MP Photo

Take a 5184 × 3456 pixel frame, the output of a common 18-megapixel sensor. The thirds lines land on whole pixels, while the phi grid uses the golden ratio of 1:1.618, which puts its lines at 38.2% and 61.8% of each side, closer to the middle:

LineRule of thirdsPhi (golden ratio)Gap
Left vertical1,728 px1,980 px252 px
Right vertical3,456 px3,204 px252 px
Top horizontal1,152 px1,320 px168 px
Bottom horizontal2,304 px2,136 px168 px

So the four thirds crossings are (1,728, 1,152), (3,456, 1,152), (1,728, 2,304) and (3,456, 2,304). Anything placed between the two sets of lines satisfies both proportions, which is why many editors treat the 252-pixel band as one target zone rather than two.

Rule of Thirds in Photography: Placing the Subject

Most photography uses the grid the same way: pick the strongest element, then decide which line or crossing it belongs on. Working photographers repeat the exercise until it becomes a habit.

Landscape Frames and the Horizon

In a landscape, put the horizon on the lower third when the sky carries the drama, or the upper third when the foreground does. A lone tree or peak goes on a crossing.

Portrait Eye Line and Looking Room

Line up the eyes on the top line; the eyes are the point of focus, not the head. Place the body in the left third when the person faces right, so the right third gives them looking room.

Architecture, Street and Film

Put a building corner or vanishing point on a crossing. On the street, a figure on one vertical with space ahead reads as motion. Cinematography uses the same rule to keep gaze and empty space on opposite sides.

When to Break the Rule of Thirds

The grid is a habit, not a law, and there are clear moments to break the rule:

  • Symmetric subjects such as a reflected lake or a frontal facade look strongest centred.
  • Repeating patterns and textures have no single point to place.
  • Tight close-ups that fill the frame make the crossings irrelevant.
  • A very small subject in a wide scene can stand out better at dead centre.

Composition Overlays in Practice: Lining Up a 4:5 Product Post

A ceramicist needs one listing shot of a speckled mug for a 4:5 Instagram post, which publishes at 1,080 × 1,350 px. The question is simple: where should the 4:5 window sit inside the original so the glossy rim highlight, the brightest point in the picture, lands on a power point? She loads the photo into this grid tool to see where the 4:5 window's lines fall. The answer turns out to be a left offset of 1,258 px, and the reason is worth following.

The phone file is 4,032 × 3,024 px. Before anything else, I mark the rim highlight with the tool: it sits at (2,871, 1,046). On the full file the right thirds line is at 2,688 px, so the highlight looks 183 px off and you would be tempted to call the shot badly composed. That reading is wrong, because the grid that matters is the one on the final 4:5 window, not the original.

  1. Full height is kept, so the window is 3,024 × 0.8 = 2,419 px wide.
  2. With a first-guess offset of 1,174 px, the highlight lands at x = 1,697 inside the window. The right thirds line sits at 2,419 × 2 ÷ 3 = 1,612.7, so it misses by 84 px, about 38 px once scaled to 1,080 wide.
  3. Vertically it sits at 1,046 against a thirds line at 1,008, a 38 px gap that shrinks to 17 px after scaling. That part is fine.
Left offsetHighlight x in windowGap to thirds lineGap to phi line (1,495)
1,174 px1,69784 px202 px
1,258 px1,6130.3 px118 px

Solving 2,871 − 1,612.7 gives the break-even offset of 1,258.3 px, and the window still fits because 1,258 + 2,419 = 3,677 px, inside the 4,032 px width. I cross-check by switching the tool to its phi layout: its right line sits at 1,495, 118 px away, so this composition is a thirds placement, not a golden-section one.

My judgement: the number to watch is the horizontal offset, not the vertical one. The 4:5 format leaves 1,613 px of sideways freedom but none vertically, so all of the composition decision happens left to right. The edge case is the profile view, where the post appears as a small preview; at that size an 84 px miss is invisible, so the careful placement pays off in the full-size listing, not the preview.

Composition Grids Beyond the Thirds

Several composition grids grew out of older proportion systems. Each answers a different question about the frame.

Phi Grid and the Golden Ratio

Phi splits each side 1 : 0.618 : 1, so its middle band is narrower than a third. Many nature shooters prefer it because the result feels calmer and less mechanical than the thirds.

Golden Triangle and Diagonal Method

The golden triangle draws one diagonal line corner to corner, then two reciprocal lines meeting it at right angles. The diagonal method uses 45-degree lines from each corner. Both build tension by placing elements along slopes.

Fibonacci Spiral

Also known as the golden spiral, it nests squares and traces curved leading lines toward one focal zone, which suits scenes with flow or movement.

Dynamic Symmetry and the Rabatment

Dynamic symmetry layers diagonals and verticals to create rhythm, popular for still-life work. The rabatment swings the short side of the frame onto the long side to mark a square.

Rule of Fifths and Center Cross

The rule of fifths divides each side into five strips for wide panoramas. A center cross simply marks the middle, useful for symmetry checks.

Choosing a Grid Overlay for Your Image

Start with thirds when you need a fast decision, then compare the golden ratio version when the focal point feels pushed too far toward the edge. A compositional grid only helps if you can see the difference: toggle between the two on the same file and keep whichever placement reads more naturally to you.

Rule of Thirds Overlay in Lightroom, Photoshop and Capture One

All three editors ship cropping guides: Lightroom cycles them with the O key, Photoshop lists them in its trim options bar, and Capture One adds them under the grid settings.

Reframe the Shot in Post

Editing gives you a second chance. Crop slightly tighter to reframe the shot onto a crossing, but remember every pixel you trim lowers the print size you can make from the image. Then load the trimmed file back into the grid tool, because the thirds and phi lines move with the new dimensions.

Grid Lines in Your Camera Viewfinder

Most cameras offer a rule of thirds grid overlay in the viewfinder or screen settings, and every smartphone has a grid switch in its camera app. Turn it on so you compose at the moment of shooting instead of fixing it later.

Using a Compositional Grid in Graphic Design and Painting

The same guide works outside photos. In graphic design and web page design, put a headline or call-to-action on a crossing and leave the rest open. For illustration and painting, sketch light thirds lines before blocking in shapes. Any design or art form that fills a rectangle, across the visual arts, can use it.

Why a Thirds Grid Feels Balanced

An off-centre subject gives the viewer's eye somewhere to travel: from the point of interest across the open area and back. That open area is negative space, and it creates balance without making the picture static. The result is usually more visually engaging than an off-center element placed at random, and more balanced than one centred by default. It remains a composition guideline, so trust what you see over the lines.

Origins of the 3x3 Grid

The idea first appears in John Thomas Smith's 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery, where he called a division in thirds the most pleasing proportion. Painters carried it into the 19th century, and photographers adopted it once grid screens arrived. That is why thirds is this tool's default layout, with phi and the diagonals as alternatives from the same proportion tradition.

Common Mistakes with a Grid Generator

  • Applying the grid before you crop. A square or 4:5 ratio moves every line, so set the final ratio first.
  • Judging at full size only. Check the thumbnail too, since most viewers see that first.
  • Forcing every element onto a crossing. One strong subject per image is plenty.

faq.question: What does a composition grid show?
faq.answer: It splits your frame with guide lines so you can see where to put the main subject. The classic rule of thirds grid uses two vertical and two horizontal lines at one-third and two-thirds of each side, which creates four intersection points.

faq.question: Is the rule of thirds a strict rule?
faq.answer: No, it is a guideline. It is a quick shortcut to an off-centre composition, but symmetric subjects, patterns and frame-filling close-ups often look better centred.

faq.question: How is the phi grid different from the rule of thirds?
faq.answer: The phi grid is based on the golden ratio and places its lines at about 38.2% and 61.8% of each side, slightly closer to the centre than the thirds lines at 33.3% and 66.7%.

faq.question: Where exactly do the intersection points go?
faq.answer: For a frame W pixels wide and H pixels tall, the rule of thirds points sit at (W/3, H/3), (2W/3, H/3), (W/3, 2H/3) and (2W/3, 2H/3). Put your focal point on the one that leaves open space on the side the subject faces.

faq.question: Should I set the grid before or after cropping?
faq.answer: After. Changing the aspect ratio moves every line, so enter the final width and height of the cropped image to get positions that match what viewers will see.

faq.question: Why does the print size change with DPI?
faq.answer: Print size is the pixel count divided by the dots per inch. The same image prints half as large at 600 DPI as at 300 DPI, so check the paper fit before exporting a gridded print.

faq.question: What are power-point zones?
faq.answer: A subject rarely sits exactly on a crossing of two thin lines, so the shaded zone around each intersection shows the area that still reads as on the point.

content_html:
Before your next call or selfie, the Live Filter Preview lets you try four webcam filters and see what brightness, contrast, saturation and blur do to your image side by side with the untouched feed. Unlike novelty webcam effects, these are tonal real-time effects, so you get a clear before-and-after answer on how to fix a dim or washed-out camera in seconds, for free.

How the Live Filter Preview Works

Click Start Camera, pick a device if you have more than one camera input, then drag the four sliders. Everything runs online with no installation and no plugin, and when the look is right you can download a still photo and save it to your computer.

Allow Access to Your Web Camera

Your browser asks once for permission; choose allow access or the web camera stays dark. There is no registration, and for privacy the stream is processed locally on your devices, never uploaded.

A Real Time Before and After Mirror

The left pane shows the raw feed and the right pane shows the filtered one, updated in real time like a mirror. If your image looks flipped or upside-down, that comes from the camera driver, not from the filters, and it affects all your photos.

Brightness, Contrast and Saturation: The Webcam Filters Explained

The four webcam filters are deliberately simple filter options that correct a photo rather than decorate it. Turn saturation to 0% and you get a true black and white picture; nothing here adds grainy texture or colour casts.

SliderRangeWhat it changes
Brightness50–150%Multiplies every channel; lifts a dark room
Contrast50–150%Pushes tones away from mid-grey
Saturation0–200%0% gives black & white, 200% doubles colour
Blur0–10 pxSoftens fine detail

The Formulas Behind Each Slider

Each slider applies the standard CSS filter maths to every pixel channel \(C\) (0–255), in this order: brightness, contrast, saturation, blur. No computer vision is involved.

$$C_{b} = C \times b \qquad C_{c} = (C - 127.5) \times c + 127.5$$ $$R_{s} = (0.213 + 0.787s)R + (0.715 - 0.715s)G + (0.072 - 0.072s)B$$

Saturation keeps luminance fixed while moving each channel toward or away from grey, which is why these effects and filters never change how bright you look.

Blur for Skin Smoothing and Touch-Ups

A 1–2 px blur gives a soft focus that hides texture, a crude version of the skin smoothing in beauty filters. It cannot add makeup or targeted touch-ups, and above 4 px it looks like bokeh on your face.

Take Photos Online With Live Filters: A Worked Example

Say your desk lamp sits behind the screen and a cheek pixel reads RGB(148, 104, 86), luminance 112.1. You set brightness 118%, contrast 106% and saturation 88% with live filters:

StepCheek pixelWall pixel
Original148, 104, 8671, 74, 83
Brightness 118%174.6, 122.7, 101.583.8, 87.3, 97.9
Contrast 106%177.5, 122.4, 99.981.2, 84.9, 96.2
Saturation 88%172, 124, 10482, 85, 95

Your skin's luminance rises from 112.1 to 132.5, while contrast pulls the darker wall back down by 2.4 levels, so you separate from the background. The 88% saturation trims the orange lamp cast without the flat look of vintage filters. One caveat: at 118% any channel above 216 clips to 255, so check a bright window before you take photos online with these settings. That does more for your confidence than any aesthetic preset.

Balancing a Window-Lit Tutoring Call With Webcam Effects

A maths tutor has a parent meeting at 4:15 on a laptop whose desk faces a north window. The question is simple: which brightness and contrast settings make both sides of the face readable without blowing out the lit side? The answer turns out to be brightness 112%, contrast 94% and saturation 104%, and the filter preview shows why before the call starts.

With the camera running, the tutor samples two spots from a downloaded still: the window-side forehead at RGB(203, 171, 152), luminance 176.4, and the shadow-side cheek at RGB(97, 72, 63), luminance 76.7. That 99.8-level gap is what makes the face look half lit.

The first instinct is brightness alone. At 112% the shadow cheek lifts to luminance 85.9, but the gap widens to 111.7, because brightness multiplies every value and bright values gain more. Dropping contrast to 94% pulls both sides toward mid-grey and brings the gap back to 105.0, with the shadow cheek at 88.4 and the forehead at 193.4. Saturation at 104% only restores a little warmth that the grey window light drains; it leaves luminance where it is.

SettingsForehead redLight/shadow gap
No filters203.099.8
112% / 100% / 104%228.5111.7
112% / 94% / 104%222.5105.0
120% / 94% / 104%237.8112.5

The cross-check is the broadcast video range in ITU-R BT.709, where 235 is reference white. Solving the same formulas for the forehead red channel shows it crosses 235 at about 119% brightness, so 120% is already past the point where compression in a meeting app tends to flatten skin into a white patch. That is the number to watch here, not the shadow side.

The caveat: this webcam filter preview only shows the result locally. The tutor's next step is to enter brightness +12 and contrast −6 in the camera's own settings, then rerun the preview at neutral sliders to confirm the raw feed now matches. If the window brightens later in the day, the forehead crosses 235 sooner, so a lamp on the shadow side fixes the gap more reliably than any slider.

Live Effects vs Photo Booth Filters, AR Lenses and Masks

An online photo booth or a webcam toy layers fun effects and digital effects on top of the image. AR lenses and AR effects use augmented reality to track your face and pin masks, hairstyles, glasses, hats or beards to it. The photo booth approach is for play; tonal filters make you look better lit.

Photo Booth Effects and Distorting Styles

Most photo booth effects fall into a few families; the right column shows what these camera filters for tone can match:

FamilyExamplesWith these sliders
Colour looksvintage, old movie, rainbow, underwater, pop art, watercolor, sketch, comic bookMuted or mono looks only
Simulated sensorsnight vision, thermal, x-rayNo
Warpsfisheye, bulge, pinch, twist, ripple, kaleidoscopeNo
Layoutssplit screen, quad camNo
Face trackingreal-time masksNo

Frames and Stickers on a Photo Strip

Here you save one still with no frames or stickers. Booth tools take four pictures about 3 seconds apart, decorate them and let you share the photo strip; a photo booth camera is built to take pictures online for fun, record videos or make GIF animations, while this preview checks selfies or a video setup.

Camera Filters for Video Calls and Streaming

For video calls and streaming, find your brightness, contrast and saturation values here, then enter them in Zoom, OBS or Discord. A virtual camera adds what this page cannot: a webcam beauty filter, a former Snap Camera lens, live effects such as neon or glitch, or a beauty filter on every frame.

Why a Preview Is Not a Virtual Camera

The Live Filter Preview never touches the feed other apps receive. Use it to find your numbers, then copy them into your meeting app or free webcam filters that do run real-time effects on the transmitted stream.

Online Camera in Any Browser on Laptop, Tablet and Phone

This online camera is cross-platform and mobile-friendly: it works in Chrome, Edge and other browsers on a desktop, laptop, tablet or phone. If it fails to start, close other apps using the camera.

faq.question: How much does the live filter preview cost?
faq.answer: Nothing. The webcam filters run free in your browser, with no account, no registration and no limit on how many stills you download.

faq.question: Do I need to install anything to use these webcam filters?
faq.answer: No. There is no installation and no plugin; the preview runs in Chrome, Edge and other current browsers on a laptop, desktop, tablet or phone.

faq.question: Why does my camera not show up?
faq.answer: Your browser has to be allowed to use the camera. Click Start Camera, choose allow access when asked, and close any other app (Zoom, Teams, OBS) that may already be holding the camera.

faq.question: Does the preview change what people see in my video calls?
faq.answer: No. It only filters the copy shown on this page. To use the look in a call, copy the brightness, contrast and saturation values into your meeting app or camera settings, or use a virtual camera app.

faq.question: Can I add stickers, frames or fun effects?
faq.answer: Not here. Photo booth tools add frames, stickers, AR masks and novelty effects such as fisheye or night vision; this tool sticks to tonal adjustments so you look natural, just better lit.

faq.question: Is my video uploaded anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The camera stream is processed locally in your browser and the downloaded still is saved straight to your device.

faq.question: Which settings fix a dark webcam image?
faq.answer: Start by raising brightness to around 110-120% and check that bright areas such as a window do not clip, then adjust contrast a few points either way and trim saturation if a lamp gives your skin an orange cast.
